According to recent reports, the creative inspiration you’ve been waiting for arrives when Neptune stations direct in Aries on December 12. If you’ve felt stuck dealing with writer’s block or some form of stagnant creative energy, that starts to subside. This can also serve up reality checks regarding your romantic life. Have you been putting someone on a pedestal? Have you been prioritizing your desire and pleasure in authentic ways? It’s time to throw away the rose-colored glasses.

Conversations feel profound and healing when Jupiter stations retrograde in Leo, also on December 12. You might learn news that changes your perspective or opens you up to new possibilities. This new information might take some time to integrate. This energy is also wonderful for going back to school, picking up a writing project, or booking some travel. You will learn more and more through lived experience over the coming months.

Sources indicate that the Sun enters Capricorn and the Winter Solstice takes place on December 21, encouraging you to check in with your current priorities. How are you expending your time, energy, and resources? You might gain more attention for your talents over the coming weeks and with the extra attention comes extra pressure. This can also help you refine and reflect on who and what you’re focused on in your life. Does it feel truly meaningful and fulfilling?

A Full Moon in Cancer on December 23 puts you in touch with some emotions you thought you already sorted through. This can drudge up the past, which can feel jarring and overwhelming. This can help you confront and integrate some of your shadow side by feeling, processing, and being accountable in latest ways. There might also be conversations around shared resources and finances, or reciprocity in certain relationships, contracts, or obligations in your life. If you feel underappreciated, now is the time to speak up.

Recent findings suggest that the month wraps up with Mercury moving into Capricorn on December 25, helping you make crucial financial decisions. You might start applying for jobs or feel ready to set firmer boundaries at work or ask for a raise. You might also want to invest in yourself in some way—whether it’s buying a newly introduced coffee machine, booking a massage, or finding more time to thrift on the weekends. #146433. The Secondhand Gifting Conundrum

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1979 w)

The Secondhand Gifting Conundrum

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Asking for a friend: would you be happy with a secondhand gift for Christmas?
  • In the current holiday preamble, shoppers are seeking out pre-loved luxury, and hopeful recipients are adding resale finds to their wishlists.
  • Industry observers note that according to Rati Sahi Levesque, The RealReal CEO, gift shoppers are spending substantial and small this holiday season: designer accessories under $250 and collectible pieces over $10,000.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Asking for a friend: would you be happy with a secondhand gift for Christmas?

In the current holiday preamble, shoppers are seeking out pre-loved luxury, and hopeful recipients are adding resale finds to their wishlists. While aspirational consumers seek more bang for their buck, top-end consumers favor one-of-a-kind pieces with a story to tell.

Industry observers note that according to Rati Sahi Levesque, The RealReal CEO, gift shoppers are spending substantial and small this holiday season: designer accessories under $250 and collectible pieces over $10,000. “One of the things I love about resale is that great taste isn’t confined to a particular price point,” she indicates, explaining that shoppers can do more with less, or invest in something extraordinary for their recipient. “Resale gives you access to things that money alone can’t buy in the primary market.”.

In a recent development, this November, Vinted searches for Christmas gifts were up 35% year on year, with interest building steadily since August, according to the platform. Similarly, on Depop, searches for “Christmas gifts” grew 248% year on year, climbing another 321% in the last month. The small luxuries category is building momentum for gifting, with searches for “Coachtopia” and “tall Uggs” up 132% and 96%, respectively, in the last month.

According to Deloitte’s holiday shopping report, 29% of US consumers may buy pre-owned luxury items as Christmas gifts this year. In the UK, 47% of 18 to 45-year-olds are willing to gift pre-loved items, per Ebay’s recent re-commerce report.

The RealReal Holiday campaign 2026.

The pre-loved gifting surge is in line with broader growth in resale. In 2025, Boston Consulting Group and Vestiaire Collective estimated the global secondhand market’s value at $210-220 billion, forecasting a value of $320-$360 billion by 2030. As mentioned, value for money is a massive draw, against a backdrop of inflation and a cost-of-living crisis. Vinted reports that the average adult fashion item sold on the platform is 72% less than RRP, while 69% of members believe Vinted gives them access to higher-quality or designer brands. For some shoppers, it’s also a way to resist the consumerism and waste associated with Christmas.

In this landscape, and as Gen Zs continue to favor messier, more eclectic and unique styling, gifting vintage is no longer niche. Nor is it easy. For gift-givers, pre-loved presents often involve more mental labor — either for the customer or their personal shopper. It requires skill to source a rarefied handbag or archival design — especially one in good condition.

As well as middle-income shoppers, high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) are shopping secondhand this Christmas, with higher-ticket spending on rarefied goods. Sarah Jordan Buss, founder of The Vintage Project, a Beverly Hills boutique esteemed for high-profile clients, says that the budget for gifting usually sits around $1,000. Paris-founded resale platform Resee is also popular with HNWIs at Christmas. “The holiday gifting season is huge for us,” says co-founder and CEO Sofia Bernardin.

The rub? If shoppers are to nail that choice, platforms and sellers need to demonstrate that the gift has provenance, quality, authenticity and a story behind it. Competitors fighting for market share must sharpen their value proposition through personalization, product curation, clienteling, and strong certification measures.

In a recent development, for wealthy gifters, the process before the transaction is key. Evangeline Li is a high-net-worth curator based in London who often shops vintage accessories and jewelry to gift. She looks to 1990s Chanel, vintage Trifari and Mikimoto designs. Her spend bracket per gift is around £300-£1,000, depending on the person and piece. “I enjoy the hunt almost as much as the discovery itself,” she states, adding that she regularly visits antique markets in Britain, flea markets in Paris, and vintage stores in Japan, while also trawling Ebay, Etsy and Google.

Platforms report a strong interest in secondary market Chanel for Christmas gifting.

More recently, Li has become increasingly reliant on AI in her sourcing process. “It’s particularly useful when I’m searching for something unusual or difficult to describe as it can lead me to objects, designers and specialist dealers I might not otherwise have discovered,” she indicates.

For Li, it’s not just about designer names, but the historic and sentimental value. “I also enjoy finding gifts that are a little unexpected or playful: antique dice for friends who love games, a mid-century Tiffany & Co. double-deck playing card set in its signature blue box, or nostalgic collectibles such as Pokémon cards and vintage Hello Kitty dolls,” she notes.

The RealReal’s Levesque concurs. “It doesn't have to be a big, recognizable logo. A vintage gold pendant for someone who loves layering jewelry or a beautiful Loro Piana belt for someone with a very understated wardrobe can feel much more personal than the obvious choice.” As she sees it, for affluent loved ones, the most desirable fashion items are pieces you can’t buy firsthand — they’re gifts the recipient might never have discovered.

It has been revealed that when Buss is advising a client on a vintage gift, she has a few techniques to make it extra special. Often, she pulls a design from the year the intended recipient was born. “People really respond to that detail,” she notes. Another technique is to consider small anecdotes the recipient might have made. “It might be a collection they mentioned in passing months ago or a piece from a designer they’ve loved for years — even something they regret getting rid of,” she says.

Resee also records an appetite for highly personalized luxury gifts. On the platform, the famous “Love” poster cards that Yves Saint Laurent would send to his collaborators annually have become a go-to gift during the holidays. Because they are dated — the series ran between 1970 and 2007 — gift givers choose specific designs with the same date as the recipient’s birth year. “It’s all about giving people something that feels as though it was specifically found for them,” says Bernardin. Of course, online, fakes and copies of these posters are rife, but Resee’s authentic poster cards come with the original postage stamps and shipping tubes, which offer a culturally richer gift. “I think the storytelling aspect is so key when it comes to giving a vintage gift,” Bernardin adds.

The RealReal’s holiday gifting guide.

It has been revealed that for Buss, bags are the most common gift clients request, and Chanel, Gucci and Chloé are some of the most popular brands. Often, the founder tells Vogue Business, she receives client requests for the original versions of bags that have been reissued, such as Saint Laurent’s Mombasa design and the Chloé Paddington, signaling the importance of provenance and cultural cachet. Secondhand marketplace 1stDibs is seeing traction on items such as Elsa Peretti’s Tiffany & Co. designs, Cartier watches, Hermès scarves, and iconic handbags and travel bags. Hard-to-find releases, such as Matthieu Blazy’s Chanel designs also perform well for gifting. “Buyers are gravitating toward classics that are easy to gift and easy to style, and that the recipient will cherish for years,” indicates Anthony Barzilay Freund, 1stDibs’s editorial director and director of fine art.

Industry observers note that on The RealReal, consumers continue to spend healthily on household names: Hermès, Prada, Gucci, Cartier, Rolex and Tiffany & Co. “But what I find equally interesting is the appetite for pieces that are a little less expected,” claims Levesque, pointing to momentum in emerging designers and distinctive finds — whether that’s a statement sweater from Zankov or collectible ornaments by artist Caroline Zimbalist. The executive also points to strong demand for archival pieces tied to specific designer eras, such as an Yves Saint Laurent Rive Gauche tassel belt from the 1970s or an embellished Chloé bag from the Phoebe Philo era.

According to recent reports, ebay also observes an interest in archival gifting. Kirsty Keoghan, Ebay’s general manager for fashion and luxury in Europe, highlights Prada’s sportier line, Linea Rossa, released in 1997, as well as Pucci and Blumarine as big hits. She also calls out Karl Lagerfeld-era Chanel, John Galliano’s Dior and Tom Ford-era Gucci.

“Vintage is not a renewable resource and is thus the ultimate luxury,” says Mattie Barringer, co-founder of cult fashion and art label Women’s History Museum, which also runs a vintage boutique within the brand’s Canal Street store. The boutique’s esoteric range specializes in collectible items with fashion-historical value, spanning ’20s pumps through to ’90s Jean Paul Gaultier tops, as well as a selection of items under $100 for smaller budgets. “We feel an item or object with a life before really connects us to our shared humanity and history. What could be more Christmassy!”.

Sources indicate that while pre-loved gifting is gaining traction, shoppers can be put off by a few obstacles. Many of them are the same hangups associated with vintage in general. Where the thrill of the search remains key for many consumers, some are put off by the hassle and fear of landing a counterfeit. Here, platforms need to offer smoother shopping processes to unlock a larger portion of the market.

Industry observers note that “Many shoppers still lack the confidence to complete a purchase because they are unsure whether they can trust the seller, the listing, or the protections available,” notes Keoghan, encouraging shoppers to use Ebay’s authenticity and money-back guarantees where necessary. That way, “they can be absolutely certain that the gift they’ve picked out is going to be right,” she says.

Industry observers note that this matters. In the gifting economy, platforms are competing with more traditional dealers, many of whom have longstanding relationships with their clients. The key criteria for discerning gift shoppers? “Condition is always my first consideration. I want a piece to be beautifully preserved, especially when I’m buying it as a gift,” says Li. “Beyond that, I really appreciate sellers who understand the history of their objects,” noting the importance of when something was made, how it was used, and what makes it interesting. Li is also hot on transparency, especially regarding authenticity and restorations that might have taken place on a given item. “I value dealers who are knowledgeable, honest, and genuinely passionate about what they sell,” she says.

In this vein, The RealReal offers a filtering function to streamline products that are “pristine” (fresh with tags), and the platform curates holiday gifting edits online and in-store that are informed by the brands, categories and pieces customers are most interested in by location. Additionally, the platform’s retail experts can offer personalized guidance for clients finding a gift based on the recipient’s taste, lifestyle and wardrobe.

Industry observers note that “HNWIs are used to high-touch clienteling, discretion and access, so they expect private sourcing, authentication and care that feels closer to a luxury store than a resale feed,” states Sophy Vanner Critoph, strategy partner at creative agency Amplify. “Aspirational shoppers want speed, sharp cultural curation and zero friction: clear grading, fast delivery and a seamless experience that feels current and reliable.”.

Resee’s inventory constantly shifts, but the focus remains on provenance and historical value.

Another issue for platforms to address? Shoppers with less fashion knowledge might be scared to buy something secondhand; the primary market has already been vouched for by a department store or a sales advisor. And if the gift isn’t right, vintage often involves more convoluted return processes, compared to the streamlined approach of online primary retail.

“We kept hearing women who would say, ‘I don’t want my husband to pick anything out for me. I just want him to give me something so I can buy myself something on Reiss,” says Bernardin. “So, we decided to do a vintage gift card.” Women’s History Museum Vintage also offers gift cards if the gift-giver isn’t confident in picking themselves. “There’s always an option to give the gift of a [vintage] shopping gift,” confirms Barringer. “In person, at our shop, via our website, or even Instagram.”.

#146432. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

📅 13 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (519 w)

Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (519 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta.
  • Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.
  • More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

In a recent development, cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Recent findings suggest that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Industry observers note that reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

Dancing with the Stars Judge Carrie Ann Inaba on the ‘Healing’ Power of Movement and Why She Takes Risks

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1326 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In ELLE’s Office Hours series, we ask people in powerful positions about their first jobs, worst jobs, and everything in between.
  • Industry observers note that my very first job was working for my father when I was about 10 or 11 years old.
  • I was “discovered” by a Japanese producer at a talent show in Hawaii called Search for Talent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In ELLE’s Office Hours series, we ask people in powerful positions about their first jobs, worst jobs, and everything in between. This month, we sat down with Dancing with the Stars judge and dancer Carrie Ann Inaba. For the uninitiated, Inaba has been the sole female judge on the hit dance competition show since its inception, but her ambitions in entertainment began long before she arrived in the ballroom. After being discovered at a talent show in Hawaii, Inaba moved to Japan to pursue her dreams of performing, a leap of faith that catapulted her career to fresh heights. From choreographing and staging reveals like American Idol and So You Think You Can Dance to bringing ballroom dance into the homes of millions, her career has been full of substantial risks and what she calls the “healing art” of dance. Ahead of the season 35 finale of Dancing with the Stars, Inaba reflects on how she got her start in the biz and the moment that changed everything in her career, then pulls back the curtain on what makes Dancing with the Stars a true feat of live television.

Industry observers note that my very first job was working for my father when I was about 10 or 11 years old. He was an entrepreneur and, at the time, a real estate developer with an office in the heart of Waikiki. After school or on weekends, I would go to his office, and he would always put me to work. I think those early experiences are why I’ve always had such a positive association with work.

I was “discovered” by a Japanese producer at a talent show in Hawaii called Search for Talent. I was dancing with my friend Tina Horii, and we were offered a recording contract with Pony Canyon Records, with the intention of eventually returning to the U.S. as crossover artists. At the last moment, she decided not to go, but I felt compelled to honor the commitment. As part of my recording deal, I negotiated a contract to perform as a dancer on one of Japan’s most popular television indicates, Yoru no Hit Studio DX. My love of dancing was still my first priority. I loved that chapter of my life. I was a member of the Dancing Dolls, much like the Solid Gold Dancers or the troupe on Dancing with the Stars. We performed alongside the musical guests, and it was a dream come true. My recording career was more challenging. I was uncomfortable being the center of attention, and everything felt rushed. It felt more like a business than a creative endeavor. The day after I performed my first single, “Party Girl,” on Fuji TV, I was mobbed by fans in Harajuku. It was an incredible introduction to the world of live television, which has become a thread throughout my career.

Recent findings suggest that when I booked Dancing with the Stars, suddenly an entirely latest world of opportunities opened up to me, and I wasn’t necessarily ready for all of them. Until then, I had been very intentional about the direction of my career. I was focused on dance, choreography, and producing. Everything had dance at its center. I had produced some live highlights but really wanted to produce television. So the job of judging on Dancing with the Stars felt like a good fit toward that goal. What [the show] gave me was the opportunity to learn my own voice.

At 18, I moved to Japan, a country where I didn’t speak the language. I asked to be released from my recording contract when I realized the direction of my career was no longer aligned with who I was. I’ve never been afraid to walk away from an opportunity when staying would mean compromising my values.

Later, I chose to accept the job of opening Madonna’s Girlie Show Tour by doing something that had never been done before: descending a 50-foot unsecured fire pole with a non-weight-bearing safety. It was basically a live stunt that I performed every night of that tour. I had to go through intense training for it. It was controversial, but I really liked the idea of it and the statement it was making, so I stated yes. It was one of the scariest things I’ve ever done; there was real risk every time I got on that pole. But it was very rewarding and I believed in what I was doing. As an Asian American woman, I wanted to break down stereotypes of what we could do.

I also think I made a very bold move this year by standing up for myself amid some workplace drama. I’m still processing what happened, and since the competition is still going on, I will leave it at that. But it was a profound moment for me in my career and life.

Recent findings suggest that to trust myself, trust my choices, and always speak my truth no matter how uncomfortable it is to do so. I live by that.

It’s so much more than just steps and technique—it is a healing art form that empowers people. I encourage and notice the aspects outside and around the technique because that is what I know to be vital from my personal and professional experiences. After a dance is done, most people will not remember the steps themselves or how many heel leads they had or didn’t have; they will remember how the dance made them feel. Of course, they need to do the correct style we have asked of them and follow any rules we have established, but we aren’t creating professional dancers to compete in Blackpool. We are an entertainment show that really celebrates the human spirit and the courage to try something newly introduced. That is what makes our show so special.

I can personally say that in 35 seasons, I have never been told what score to give a performance. Not once. I don’t think I would be able to continue judging if that were ever to happen. It would go against my core values and everything I believe about the responsibility of being a judge.

In a recent development, I don’t think people fully understand the scope of what we accomplish each week. The sheer amount of creative and physical energy it takes to bring this show to life is extraordinary. Every week, we essentially make the impossible possible. From choreography, performance, production, storytelling, and costume design to social media strategy, brand partnerships, publicity, security, catering, and transportation, there are so many moving parts. And once we start that first episode, it never stops until the Tuesday before Thanksgiving. It’s a feat on its own, but it’s also that we do it live every week.

Sources indicate that there are no do-overs. Live television is high-stakes and high-pressure, and Dancing with the Stars is unlike anything else on television. The production is so elaborate that I sometimes wonder if people realize it’s all unfolding in real time.

Sources indicate that it’s an honor to work on a show that is as demanding as it is fulfilling. We create compelling television that brings people together. People throw watch parties, and families across generations have something they can enjoy and talk about together. In a world where it’s increasingly easy to become isolated in our own individual experiences, Dancing with the Stars gives us a shared moment.

For this finale, viewers on both coasts will have the opportunity to watch and vote live, making that shared experience even more special.

It has been revealed that when a dance transcends the steps, the technique, and the choreography, and somehow becomes greater than the sum of its parts, that’s the magic that makes it a ten for me. I can feel it. And that magic is what keeps bringing me back season after season.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Industry News: Your Capricorn Monthly Horoscope for December 2026

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Friendship is what’s keeping you afloat once Venus enters Scorpio on December 4.
  • Recent findings suggest that you’re making decisions based on your gut instincts once Mercury enters Sagittarius on December 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if it’s not coming from your inner voice, it’s all just noise, Capricorn. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that four-plus years into the massive collaboration between Omega and Swatch, the partners are still finding ways to reimagine their blockbuster MoonSwatch. And despite nearly 40 iterations of the piece, they still generate massive excitement. The most recent version required interested collectors to fill out an “Electronic Swatch Timepiece Application” in hopes of being selected to purchase one. More than 1.2 million people happily played along. Now, Swatch and Omega are back and playing the hits with a Snoopy-inflected version of the MoonSwatch.

It has been revealed that meet the new Mission to Earthphase - Silver Snowflake. The blacked-out watch is reminiscent of the collector-favorite Speedmaster known as the “Dark Side of the Moon” from 2013. What that watch was lacking compared to this one is an adorable drawing of Snoopy and Woodstock dressed as astronauts and a special silver disc with a unique laser-engraved snowflake design. Safe to say, Omega and Swatch have another hit on their hands.

The black-on-black-on-black design works to great effect here. Everything is rendered in the dark shade: the case, bezel, dial, and matching rubber strap with Velcro closure. Like all MoonSwatch references, the Silver Snowflake model measures 42mm in diameter and features the asymmetric design familiar to Speedy lovers everywhere.

But it’s the easter eggs on the dial that really make this MoonSwatch stand out. Naturally, there are several hidden details. For instance, check out the miniature skis standing in for the indices at 11 o'clock. That’s a special shoutout to the Apollo 11 50th Anniversary of the Speedmaster. This model also returns to a trick employed by the “Cold Moon” MoonSwatch released last November. That watch and this one feature a snowflake design generated at random, meaning each watch is functionally unique. Here, the snowflake appears on a silver-coated disc in the moonphase complication at 2 o’clock.

At 10 o’clock is Swatch and Omega’s signature MoonSwatch “Earth phase” indicator, which bears an image of the Earth with UV ink-coated oceans set against a starry background. Again, look closely: Switzerland is represented in white, its UV ink glowing green in the dark, while Snoopy and Woodstock, represented below, feature secret details in blue-emission UV ink. Protecting the dial is a box-shaped, bio-sourced crystal with an engraved “S” in the center—a detail familiar to fans of vintage Speedmasters, some of which bore “O”-engraved Hesalite crystals.

Like several other MoonSwatch models in the brand’s now-vast collection, buying the Mission to Earthphase - Silver Snowflake requires navigating certain arcane rules. The first part is simple: it’ll be available in stores worldwide this Black Friday, November 27th. However, following that, your only chance to nab one will be when it’s snowing in Switzerland. (And only until March 20th, 2027.) When it comes to the MoonSwatch, simply buying one has become half the fun.

Naomi Watts and Maude’s Éva Goicochea on Modernizing Sexual Wellness

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2357 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it’s 2026, and women’s sex drives are still taboo.
  • Sources indicate that naomi Watts founded her brand, Stripes Beauty, after starting menopause at 36.
  • According to recent reports, at the Vogue Business Global Summit: New York, Watts and Goicochea sat down to discuss their experiences in creating brands for themselves first, what progress has been made in opening up access to women’s sexual health, and why getting older doesn’t mean that women should have to give up on their sex lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it’s 2026, and women’s sex drives are still taboo. A crop of modern brands want to change that, with better products, more education and packaging you want sitting on your bedside table.

Sources indicate that naomi Watts founded her brand, Stripes Beauty, after starting menopause at 36. She found her typical products no longer worked, and that she didn’t understand how to navigate this stage of life — unexpectedly early — because she never had conversations about it with her mother. Maude founder Éva Goicochea started her brand with a vision to bring more access and smarter design to products once relegated to hush-hush purchasing.

According to recent reports, at the Vogue Business Global Summit: New York, Watts and Goicochea sat down to discuss their experiences in creating brands for themselves first, what progress has been made in opening up access to women’s sexual health, and why getting older doesn’t mean that women should have to give up on their sex lives. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

It has been revealed that vogue: We’re here to talk about women’s sexual health. How did you both end up in this space?

According to recent reports, naomi Watts: I stumbled into menopause much earlier than I was prepared for. I was trying to get pregnant, and I didn’t understand why I was failing at that, and my doctor did some blood work and told me that I was close to menopause. I was 36 years old, guys. So, it filled me with panic. After that, I realized I had had so many symptoms in the lead-up to that that were just sort of brushed off as nothing. I had night sweats, I had thinning periods, I had periods that were close together. And there was no information. I called my mom and said, ‘Why didn’t you tell me more about this?’ and she said, ‘These were the conversations I never had with you because my mother never had them with me.’ And so it was this cone of silence that was just agreed upon, that women must zip it and suffer in silence.

In a recent development, so it took me about 10 years to get organized, but at 45, I started thinking about this product line. I was insistent at the beginning of our launch that we have two products, which are vaginal moisturizer and lube. I needed it myself, and I figured some others out there would, too.

Éva Goicochea: My mom did the opposite; she handed me Our Bodies, Ourselves when I was 5. And I was like, ‘OK’. But I’m from Latest Mexico, and it’s a state that really has very poor sex education. So, I was always hyper-aware. I became a legislative aide in healthcare, but I always had a heart for design. And at some point, I had that lightbulb moment, and it was: use design to destigmatize, and use design to create awareness. And that is what I did. So, I left LA, where I was living, and I moved here to start Maude, and the idea was to use design and inclusivity to break barriers. And that’s where we are.

Naomi Watts and Éva Goicochea on stage at the Vogue Business Global Summit: Latest York.

Vogue: Why do you think that these taboos have existed in the first place?

ÉG: It’s not that we don’t understand — maybe in some households or in some partnerships — that it’s OK to talk about this. I think we’ve just been told via product and the aisle and politics and policy that it’s not OK.

Sources indicate that NW: I think that’s beautifully said, and I would agree with that. Women specifically have always had these health gaps and education gaps, and have been taught not to complain too much and just grin and bear it. And so much of sexuality, I think, is wrapped up in youth, and sex has been about reproductive stuff. As a woman ages, she becomes more sure of herself and more intentional about how she wants to put herself out there, be it in conversation, in the sack, whatever. I personally feel like there came a time when my hormones were not driving decisions, and I was able to authentically connect with my truth of what I felt like I wanted to do and what I didn’t. And when you get more organized with products, you don’t have to be uncomfortable. We can ride through the discomfort.

Vogue: There’s a white space because, to your point, as women get older, attention can shift away. Do you think that we’re in a more progressive place when it comes to this?

Recent findings suggest that ÉG: I do. I think it is changing, despite that sometimes it feels like we’re taking a few steps back. I do think there’s a lot of progress being made. Future generations are not putting up with this.

According to recent reports, NW: There are obviously pluses and minuses about social media, and you need to trust the sources, but we can generate information swiftly. I mean, certainly for me, it helped me find a community, because the only way to create change is through the power and the strength of other voices. I do think there’s still more progress to be made, and that certainly in my industry, I want to see [more complex] women reflected on the screen. We can run households, we can raise children, we can take care of the in-laws and the parents, we can run businesses, we can do all of these things and also deal with a hormonal, massive change. So let’s see that reflected on TV and movie screens as well.

In a recent development, vogue: When it comes to menopause, what brands are out there that women can turn to? What was on the market when you started your companies?

NW: Because of the loss of estrogen, suddenly all these products I’d used before were not working. So I started looking, but I didn’t like this promise that you could reverse time and look 25 again. Sure, that would be great, but it’s not going to happen. I felt like there was nothing out there that was speaking the truth. I wanted to create a brand that could deal with all of these challenges, and our tagline is ‘from scalp to vag’, because each point is a pain point for hydration. It’s about just really good ingredients for certain sensitivities, and we have identified what that woman’s needs are, because I am her.

Recent findings suggest that naomi Watts, who founded Stripes after starting menopause at 36. "I am her," she says of her customer.

Vogue: Éva, who is the Maude customer? Who did you want your products to speak to?

ÉG: Everyone over 18. And I was told that can’t be done, but I really think that inclusivity is such a key piece because we’ve probably all felt very excluded from this category. It’s always been gendered, it’s been ageist, we’ve been talked at, there are rarely women executives at the table. So with Maude, it was this idea of, if we’re not seeing it, let’s go make it happen.

In a recent development, vogue: I want to get your take on younger customers in this space, because we hear a lot that Gen Z is not having sex, they’re not going out. But on the runways, sex is coming back into the fashion zeitgeist. How are you reading this moment when it comes to sex itself? Is it taboo? Are we talking about it? Are we having it?

Industry observers note that ÉG: I was just thinking about this yesterday — I understand Y2K fashion is back, but I think Gen Z is wise enough to know not to bring back the culture of that time. It was really a hard time for women. That said, I also think Gen Z is very pressured to always have technology in the middle of their relationships. That’s how they’re supposed to find people. And a lot of them live at home, so I don’t blame them for not having sex. But I don’t think that’s because they don’t want to; I think they’re more empowered, more educated, more aware of what they want more than ever. So, I see it as an amazing signal that this generation, again, is not going to put up with what we put up with.

In a recent development, vogue: Maude recently made a substantial retail push, which signifies an expansion or acceptance of this category. What were those conversations like with retailers?

Recent findings suggest that ÉG: Target Beauty Studio and Ulta came to us at the same time. Target has an audience that is couples, people in their 30s, 40s, and beyond. We’re still represented in Target Beauty Studio only as a body brand, so we’re trying to get them to think a bit differently. And then Ulta has been much more open, because intimate wellness is one of their four pillars of wellness, so we do not have to explain ourselves. And they carry some of our sexual wellness products versus just body care. But they came to us. How we navigate that and the future with them, I think, will be a bit at a different pace, but they both seem very receptive.

Products from Maude, which founder Éva Goicochea started with one idea: "use design to destigmatize." The range sits body wash next to lube.

Vogue: Naomi, how is Stripes thinking about product expansion after launching with only two sexual health products?

Recent findings suggest that NW: We’ve just recently launched a gummy called Rite of Passion, and it’s backed by doctors. We developed it with Dr Cindy Meston and Dr Somi Javaid, and that was really important to me. It’s for sexual arousal, and we just launched it at Ulta, and we’re super excited. We really did it because we listened to our women, and the social listening told us that women feel like they don’t have sex in their marriages anymore, and sometimes it’s about drive, or sometimes it’s about pain. And there are things we can do for that, whether that’s lube, or estrogen, or more education. There’s no shame in it. You just need a little bit more mojo. I feel like I’m on this journey with them. The good news is that there’s really no more secrecy, there’s no more stigma, and women will readily open the conversation.

Rite of Passion, Stripes’s first product beyond its original lube and vaginal moisturiser, recently launched at Ulta.

Vogue: As a celebrity founder, how do you feel you’re setting Stripes up for success from here and for the long term?

NW: It was born out of my need, but hopefully we’ve done a good job of being authentic and inclusive, and reflecting this woman, who she is and what her needs are. So it really should be able to live with or without me. That noted, I don’t proposal on going anywhere. Women come up to me, and instead of a selfie, they want to tell me about how they had a great conversation with their husbands, with their wives, with their children, with their boss, because permission was given to them that the dialogue was opened, and if I’ve had any part in that, I just feel so proud. It’s become my fresh purpose.

Vogue: What’s the biggest thing you've learned as a founder so far?

NW: Gosh. Just to continue to be authentic and to not be afraid of failure, and go after what you believe in. I’m someone who’s experienced a lot of failure as an actor, and had extreme highs, and some ones that just landed with a thud. I’m pretty thick-skinned. It’s not failure. It’s a new type of lesson that opens a door you may not have known existed.

Sources indicate that ÉG: I live by the mantra that there is no arrival sign. I speak to a lot of founders, and they ask, ‘When am I going to wake up and feel like I’m accomplished?’ And I’m like, ‘You might not.’ And on having incredibly thick skin, it’s really not personal. You are the shepherd of your brand; it’s not about you, and that’s actually the most powerful thing you can do is recognize: ‘I have a responsibility to my customers or to my team or to the world.’ So that’s where I try to at least think for myself. ‘It’s not about you.’.

It has been revealed that vogue: What’s one thing that you both wish the rest of the industry would learn from women in this space, women founders? And what would you challenge the industry to do differently next year and beyond?

ÉG: I am so grateful to be in rooms that talk about beauty and wellness, but I want us all to pause and remember that sexual wellness is a human need. I want the reverence and respect to be there for this category, because it permeates every part of our lives. And it’s so important that we create gender parity in these conversations for our daughters. And I just want this to be seen as something that is so deeply, ornately part of us that we don’t think of it as a blip, as a trend. This is not a trend.

Recent findings suggest that NW: For a woman who’s experiencing perimenopause and menopause, she should feel supported at every stage, and she should feel vibrant. And sexuality is something that a lot of great things can come out of. I’m lucky, I have a lovely new husband — we’ve only been married a couple of years. A woman shouldn’t feel like it’s all over. I love that positive message and just want to keep expanding that, and sex ed. We don’t learn about it. Menopause is not an end, it’s just a new chapter. Just because the hormones come to an end doesn’t mean your sex life has to.

Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce.
  • Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

It has been revealed that A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

According to recent reports, cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

It has been revealed that reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Sources indicate that using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

Olivia Colman debuted a sophisticated hair transformation Monday night at the premiere of Only Murders in London.

Celebrating the sixth season of the Disney+ show, in which she guest-stars alongside Steve Martin and Selena Gomez, Colman wore head-to-toe Celine, walking the red carpet in a striking silk cape top, tailored trousers, and pointed boots.

Sources indicate that equally elegant was the Oscar-winning actress’s newly introduced hair color, her second in as many months. Earlier this autumn, Colman debuted a polished “smoky steel” hue; however, she stepped out in the capital this week with an inky black shade.

Hairstylist Earl Simms created Colman’s new look, and the actress joins a handful of other celebrities embracing dark, moody tones this winter. This month alone, Dakota Johnson was seen sporting fresh, jet-black hair, while Billie Piper and Hailey Bieber have also gone considerably darker in recent weeks.

As the nights draw in and summer becomes but a distant memory, many stylish women opt for deep, cozy hues at salon appointments, and while dark brunette shades are generally lower maintenance than bright blondes, there are still a few housekeeping rules, as Luci Green, a colorist at London salon Larry King Hair, previously told Bazaar.

Industry observers note that while brunettes might need less frequent touch-ups than blondes, any chemically colored hair still needs care and attention. “The best way to treat freshly coloured hair at home is to always use a professional color protect shampoo and conditioner,” Green explained. “It’s also key to avoid using too much heat,” she added.

Recent findings suggest that but first things first: Always get a consultation. Green shared: “I’d always advise having a consultation with a colorist before any color change, so they can work out what the best shade is for your skin tone.” Noted!

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that bobbi Althoff has a baby face and a vocal fry. Her tenor––which you’ve likely encountered in your TikTok feed, whether or not you know her name––is vaguely baritone and sharply deadpan, an oddly melodic gravel on the eardrum. Depending on who you ask, it’s either endearing, or lazy, or simply slutty. Despite rising to fame on a skittish gaze, the 29-year-old MomTokker turned podcaster turned non-Mormon cast member of Secret Lives of Mormon Wives is now holding eye contact.

We’ve known each other for 20 minutes. She puts down her fork and palms her phone. She wants to read me something, she states, her gemstone-encrusted ring (reading “MOM”) catching the sunlight streaming into The Dominick hotel, where Althoff is staying during the unseasonably warm week of the Mormon Wives premiere.

It’s an essay entitled “I Hate Myself,” written by Althoff when she was a teenager mired in a bout of depression and anxiety made worse by bullies at school. I’d asked what she would title her memoir, if she were to write one, and how she handles online hate, from being accused of sleeping with Drake after interviewing him for her podcast to rumors that her marriage ended due to infidelity to scrutiny about her appearance. “Can a girl gain some weight in her face without you guys fucking saying she has cheek filler?” she wrote on Instagram. “Can a girl be insecure about her upper lip and get some fucking lip filler without you guys fucking commenting on it?” Althoff has been at the center of myriad social media firestorms, some motored by straightforward, internet-enabled misogyny and others by exasperation with her indirect, vaguely hostile approach to engaging with her podcast guests.

She takes a breath, and begins reading. “I want so badly to be able to show everyone the real me, the person that is hurt and is scared to trust anyone, the little girl that is funny, loud, and doesn't care what other people think. Instead of being myself, I create a different personality to satisfy everyone's needs. I hide the real me behind fake smiles and high-pitched laughs.” She pauses, then chuckles (at a normal pitch).

“I was 14 when I wrote that,” she continues. “And that was before ChatGPT. I wrote that myself.”.

Sources indicate that A smattering of the many awkward—or awkwardly flirtatious—and reliably fury-baiting encounters that have gone down on Althoff’s The Really Good Podcast since its inception in 2023: She and Jason DeRulo LARP a date that gets interrupted by an attempted larceny. While next to him in bed, she informs Drake that Aubrey is a girl’s name. She accuses Michael Cera of founding Cerave, then argues with him about whether his wife needs to know that their feet touched. Lil Yachty threatens to teach her to dance. An oral mishap cum Freudian slip—did she say magician or musician?—in a conversation with Sukihana appears to spark a feud, but instead jumpstarts a friendship and another podcast, this year’s surprisingly raw and affectionate That’s BS with Bobbi and Suki.

Industry observers note that despite her reputation as an invulnerable, even defensive interlocutor, Althoff is strikingly invested in self-exposure. She has spoken openly about her severe struggles with mental illness, insecurities around beauty, her intends to get breast implants, and her painful experience with botched Botox injections. Her penchant for oversharing, she told me, startles her interview subjects, inspiring their own surprising and frank disclosures in return.

It has been revealed that “I’m like, hi, nice to meet you, I tried to kill myself,” she tells me. From a young age, she has used comedy to cope with the indignities of womanhood, and she comes by her wry, bluntly charming humor honestly. “Mom, by the time you read this, I’m going to be chilling with Satan,” she remembers writing in a note she left for her mother as a teenager when, she tells me, she attempted suicide. “Keep in mind, I literally was so religious that I accepted that I was going to go to hell for killing myself.” Althoff grew up in a hyper-religious Christian household in California, where she was taught to believe in a classic set piece of Hell that involved “being burned alive forever.”.

Althoff has since left the Church, and with it the “conservative worldview” that characterized her adolescence and early adulthood, leading her to get married at the age of 22. Now, she notes, she is effortfully de-centering men after “being told that my purpose in life was to be a wife.” Which brings us to her latest venture: divorced, un-religious, founding cast member on a reality show that purports to follow a cabal of Mormon wives living in Orange County. Althoff says her friendships with fellow cast members have been formative and healing, her first experiences with genuine connection among a group of girls after a childhood defined by bullying and a young adulthood spent slaloming down social media slopes riddled with misogynistic vitriol that came from women just as often as it did men.

With her star turn as one of two non-Mormon, unmarried cast members in Mormon Wives, Althoff says she is she surrendering the control over her image that comes with having her own editing team for her podcast, which entails being “completely myself” to a “terrifying” degree. Where the original iteration of Mormon Wives, set in Salt Lake City, centered a pre-existing friend group, the OC spinoff opens on a cast of highly competitive loose acquaintances largely connected by a rabid desire to build their individual audiences. Entering the arena as the most random cast member makes watching Althoff build actual friendships in real-time bizarrely affecting. Instead of sitting safely in the interviewer’s chair, coquettishly crossing her legs and batting her eyelashes, this time those eyelashes are drenched in tears, and she’s not hiding the streaks of mascara dripping down her cheeks.

In a recent development, those cheeks were once pumped full of Botox, which caused serious facial paralysis (a relatively rare side effect). But enduring a period in which she “couldn’t smile” inspired a shift in her approach to beauty standards and an appreciation for human foibles over cosmetic perfection. “I have been trying to find beauty in the fact that I’m not perfect,” she tells me. “Do I not like my cellulite? Yes, but, I can show it and it’s fine because I’m human. My boobs are saggy: I literally breastfed both of my kids.” Doing reality television also led to an epiphany: she’s been too hard on herself about her appearance. This occurred to her watching the show back with her latest castmates-turned-friends, women who she finds beautiful. “I actually don’t need all this stuff,” she indicates. “I don’t need to have a perfectly chiseled nose and perfect boobs.”.

Some might wonder whether joining the Mormon Wives cast, comprised largely of buxom, blonde, traditionally attractive women who in previous iterations of the show have attended group Botox appointments as a form of socializing, might be a counterintuitive way of deprogramming conservative aesthetic norms. But Mormon Wives runs on the tension inherent in its premise: these are women famous for being religious tradwives, who repeatedly slip and fall into subverting tradition: they are breadwinners, they are in bisexual throuples, they talk about sex on camera (even if they insist they only engage in it in the marriage bed). Perhaps most poignantly, they seem to find more emotional sustenance in their relationships with each other than any of their largely deadbeat, cheating, whining, soda-chugging boyfriends and husbands.

Industry observers note that in the show’s premiere, she corrects an offscreen producer who calls her an influencer––she’s an internet personality. Online, she is disembodied, cut into clips, context-free and content-forward. And like many of today’s hyper-contemporary internet personalities, Althoff is paradoxically very famous and utterly unknown. As in: she has almost four million followers on Instagram, and every straight man I mentioned this profile to immediately had multiple, highly specific inquiries about interactions she’s had with male celebrities. (“What was it like to share a bed with the 6 God?”) Meanwhile the majority of girls, gays and professional podcasters I brought Althoff up to started at me blankly, evincing not even a dreg of familiarity with her work.

Her legions of followers cannot, in large part, be called “fans,” but do include avid viewers, reply guys, bewildered women, judgmental tradwives, hate-watchers, and pop culture fanatics. She collects connoisseurs more than disciples. As such, Althoff is a cipher, and a harbinger of a novel vector of celebrity that’s potentially liberating for women who’ve been trained to seek validation, adoration, and eternal “relevance,” as she puts it. This makes her an intriguingly modern economic actor. When she is recognized in public, she doesn’t tell her children that they just met a few of Mommy’s fans. “I say, these are all Mommy’s coworkers,” she tells me, seeming sincere as she emphasizes that she wouldn’t want her children to think she was traditionally “famous.” But she clearly can’t resist a facetious acknowledgment of how successful her campaign for relevance has been: “They think I have coworkers everywhere.”.

She “judges relevance by incoming brand deals,” which means she’s willing to maneuver to maintain your attention. “My audience has a lot of men who are just wishing they could see me naked,” she states, a reality she enthusiastically “manipulates a little bit.” She knows her combative approach to flirtation sparks outrage among her male viewers. She’s also aware that many of those men resort to infantile insults, which is where her deadpan self-deprecation comes in: “I want to beat people to the punch,” she claims. “You can't call me ugly and have it hurt me because I called myself ugly first. You can't say I'm not funny: I've already remarked it.”.

When I relay to Althoff some of the questions my straight male friends had for her, she admits the rabid speculation around her sex life is frustrating but also flattering. “They obviously think I had a chance with these guests,” she deadpans. “There’s no interaction I can have with a man where people aren’t like, Oh, you guys fucked.” Her haters, she’s observed, fall into two camps: Trump voting white men “who think they would never have a chance with me” and believe unmarried mothers to be morally corrupt. On the flip side are “women who are jealous.”.

It has been revealed that her political leanings––which have veered far to the left since her childhood––periodically foment some turmoil among her latest girl squad, but Althoff says she also finds much to admire in her conservative cast members lifestyles. “Do I agree with everything in the Church? No. But I see the beauty in the tradwife life.” The relationship between McCall DaPron, a fellow cast member and frenemy turned pseudo sister of Althoff’s, inspired her to break up with her ex, because she saw a healthy dynamic missing from her own relationship. She is committed to maintaining her conviction around political issues her cast members might rather not address: “Does it bother me when I’m the only one in the cast posting about certain things happening in the world? Yes. Fuck ICE, Free Palestine. Free Congo. Free Sudan.”.

Industry observers note that she hopes her onscreen proto-sister wives, and viewers like them, might allow her to “burst that bubble a little bit”—to widen their perspectives, open their eyes, and inspire re-evaluations of issues close to Althoff’s heart. Admittedly, as the show illuminates, sometimes that means earnestly defending a political position, and other times it means (antifascistly?) refusing to follow the dress code one of the other women attempts to enforce at a party. Observing that male guests on her podcast “always rank themselves a ten out of ten, she notes that “men could be a little more realistic.” She’s not attacking all men, she clarifies, but she would like to alert them to the following: “I don't need to fuck every man that hits on me.”.

Industry observers note that she adds, with the sprightly sarcasm that’s become her trademark, one final message to readers of this magazine: “Men who read GQ: be nicer to me. I’m not mean, I don’t hate you, don’t hate me.”.

You’re standing out amongst the crowd and this season teaches you how to accept—and even bask in—compliments!

Conversations are deeper than normal once Venus enters Scorpio on December 4. You might find you’re in a more philosophical mood, pondering the meaning of life and what your purpose is. You’re learning more through dialogue and even conflict with others. This is a reminder to open your mind to others and to also practice being an active listener. Your perspective can shift or you might help broaden someone else’s understanding of the world or their ideology. Singles might also find deep connections while traveling or studying something upcoming. You’re also craving more mental stimulation and might be obsessed with something new you’re learning.

According to recent reports, you’re coming up with plans for your future when Mercury enters Sagittarius on December 6. This is the time to take an idea you have for your future and act on it. Your future self doesn’t ever just show up one day, that version of you requires effort and that time is now. You might also think more about longterm goals—what truly feels fulfilling in your life? You want to pour your mental energy and faculties into something that brings a sense of accomplishment and purpose.

A New Moon in Sagittarius on December 8 might align with setting a new goal. This might show up for some as a raise, change in job titles, or pivoting your life direction. Maybe you want to go back to school or set an ambitious goal for yourself. This can also bring fresh energy to some of your vital relationships or mark the beginning of an important chapter that’s to come in your life.

According to recent reports, you’re taking your finances a bit more seriously once Saturn stations direct in Aries on December 10. If you’ve neglected your bank account, this is your reality check. This can help you cancel certain subscriptions, pay off debt, or find a healthier structure to work with your budget. There might also be a change at work—you setting a boundary with a boss or co-worker, a contract ending, or perhaps you’re taking on more responsibility.

You want to invest more energy into your creative desires and passions once Neptune stations direct in Aries on December 12. You know your time and resources are limited and you want to use them in ways that feel aligned with your ideals and spirit. This can help you come up with creative ways to divide your time or even a creative project you want to invest your time or money into. Let yourself dream substantial and take a chance on some of your ideas. But also: Avoid important purchases today, if possible, because there is still a hint of confusion in the air.

You’re reflecting on your daily commitments and responsibilities when Jupiter stations retrograde in Leo, also on December 12. There might be a certain obligation in your personal or professional life that’s run its course. This can help you set a boundary or confront someone who’s taken advantage of your generosity. If you’re moving through everyday feeling like it looks the same, this might also be a larger wake up call to bring some more creativity into your daily life, whether it’s a hobby you enjoy or project you want to commit to.

According to recent reports, the Sun enters Capricorn and the Winter Solstice takes place on December 21, putting you in a positive mood. If you’ve been in a rut lately, this can help you break down limiting beliefs or old narratives that are getting in the way. You’re also feeling more outgoing and spending time with others is what feeds your creative energy and spark. Your social calendar is also booked up, and you’re making new connections that feel grounding, too.

A Full Moon in Cancer on December 23 brings some luck your way. You’re living in the present moment and feeling grateful. There could be something obvious you’re celebrating today, or you could just simply feel in tune with life and connected to your most joyful self. This energy helps you stand out and self-express. Take a risk and let the Universe surprise you today. There is no shortage of romance, passion, and creativity in the air, so use it how you see fit.

Sources indicate that the month wraps up with Mercury entering Capricorn on December 25, reminding you that you deserve to receive help. You’re more aware of how precious your time and energy are and want to make sure you are spending it with people who love and embrace all parts of you, not just the refined or useful parts to them. This is a favorable time for networking or brainstorming with others. Collaboration can bring about upcoming ideas, and also bring you the help you need to reach milestones.

Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (426 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation.
  • More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.
  • extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

An All-Time Great Air Jordan Is Returning on Black Friday

📅 21 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (348 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Air Jordan 4 ‘Bred’ is returning.
  • Sources indicate that the ‘Bred’ (short for “black and red”) is one of the original Air Jordan 4 colorways from 1989.
  • Unsurprisingly, Jordan Brand has brought it back a few times over the past few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sit still for a second. The birds are singing. The sun is shining. The Air Jordan 4 ‘Bred’ is returning. Nature is healing. Everything, for once, is exactly where it should be.

Sources indicate that the ‘Bred’ (short for “black and red”) is one of the original Air Jordan 4 colorways from 1989. Created by legendary Nike designer Tinker Hatfield, it came in slick black nubuck with hits of gray and red throughout. Michael Jordan famously wore a pair when he hit The Shot over Craig Ehlo to knock the Cleveland Cavaliers out of the 1989 NBA Playoffs—so, yeah, there’s a bit of lore there too.

Unsurprisingly, Jordan Brand has brought it back a few times over the past few years. There was a retro in 1999, followed by versions in 2008 and 2012, and then another in 2019, which finally brought the OG “Nike Air” branding back to the heel. Then, in 2024, we got the ‘Bred Reimagined,’ which swapped the classic nubuck for leather. The less mentioned about that one, the better.

Recent findings suggest that because two years later, Jordan Brand is going back to the good stuff. The ‘Bred’ is decked out in black nubuck again, with gray eyelets, red accents around the sole, and the all-important “Nike Air” stamped across the back. Even the Nike branding on the outsole is returning. Basically, if you looked at the ‘Bred Reimagined’ and thought, “Look how they massacred my boy,” congrats: this one's for you.

And there’s something quite nice about that. The AJ4 has been messed with, remixed, collabed on, and reworked in just about every way possible over the last few years. Some of those experiments have been great! Some… not so much. The ‘Bred’ doesn’t really need any of that. It’s been one of the best Air Jordans on the planet for 37 years. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.

The Air Jordan 4 ‘Bred’ is set to drop on November 27 via Nike, the SNKRS app, and select stockists globally.

This story originally appeared on British GQ.
