Latest Update: Christopher Bailey on His Post-Burberry Reinvention at the Historic Burleigh Pottery

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1674 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in Stoke-on-Trent one balmy day this summer, a Victorian world unfurled at an earthenware manufacturer I had come to visit.
  • The pottery has surrendered its photogenic aspects to a TV production crew, intent on making it an authentic, bustling 19th-century scene, but Burleigh’s story began about 40 years before this state-of-the-art manufactory was completed, in 1851, as Hulme & Booth.
  • Bowls come out of the dipping house before their final firing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in Stoke-on-Trent one balmy day this summer, a Victorian world unfurled at an earthenware manufacturer I had come to visit. Middleport Pottery, the Grade II*-listed home of Burleigh Pottery, built in 1888, is seemingly unchanged since then, as women mill around its cobbled walkways wearing patched crinoline skirts and poke bonnets, and men model timeworn top hats and darned waistcoats. An embarrassment of wooden stalls with a panoply of foodstuffs, including a rather fly-friendly table of fish, moulder in the midday sun, while an assortment of mismatched Victorian underwear hangs to dry.

The pottery has surrendered its photogenic aspects to a TV production crew, intent on making it an authentic, bustling 19th-century scene, but Burleigh’s story began about 40 years before this state-of-the-art manufactory was completed, in 1851, as Hulme & Booth. When William Leigh and Frederick Rathbone Burgess took over in 1862, it became known as Burgess & Leigh, and the abbreviated name, Burleigh, was adopted in 1903.

Bowls come out of the dipping house before their final firing.

Recent findings suggest that in 2010, it was acquired by British ceramics company Denby and, that same year, the Prince’s Regeneration Trust stepped in with a substantial £9 million sum to purchase and save the building from severe disrepair. The Prince of Wales (now King Charles III) visited the site in 2013, returning five more times. Since then, its history has been mixed, until it was recently threatened with closure. Sixty-two jobs at risk; the only pottery in the world to use underglaze tissue printing, whereby potters apply designs to vessels using tracing paper, its lengths almost hemming them in like a Victorian laundry. (Such is the commitment to this 1750s-born craft that one woman has an elaborate web of tattoos—taken from a Burleigh design—on her calves, which peeks out of her shorts as she works.).

According to recent reports, in 2018, Christopher Bailey had given up his roles of chief creative officer and president of Burberry, where he had transformed the brand since 2001 (after stints at Gucci with Tom Ford, and Donna Karan), to focus on his all-enveloping private life. “I had always hoped to have children but never actually—certainly growing up as a young gay man in quite a tough part of Yorkshire—thought that would even be within the realms of possibility,” notes Halifax-born Bailey, who is now based in Oxfordshire. “And then [I was] able to have a family and get married to a man [actor Simon Woods] and go on my Burberry adventure and all these things, these amazing, happy accidents.” Giving up his high-powered job gave him time to lavish on his girls, Iris and Nell, now in their pre-teens.

Biscuit selector Shirley inspects, brushes, and tings each piece.

One spring Sunday afternoon this year, after his husband had departed for France to shoot a film for several weeks, Bailey was walking his dog Beckett with his children. He received a phone call from a friend, who told him the news that Denby had entered administration. “I knew the product,” states Bailey. “And I noted, ‘I don’t have an emotional affinity with Denby. But let me look into it because maybe there’s more to it than I understand.’ I finished the walk and couldn’t stop thinking about it… I realized that Denby was the parent firm for Burleigh. I’ve always loved Burleigh.” (At the age of 17, Bailey had worked for a wedding dress company in Hebden Bridge, just outside Halifax, “in one of those extraordinary buildings”—so the industrial Victorian style of the 1880s Burleigh workshop was familiar to him.) By June, it was revealed that Bailey had acquired the company, alongside a small group of private investors.

Recent findings suggest that jemma Baskeyfield, the brand marketing manager, retail manager, and company historian who has been at the firm for 26 years, was practically the first person Bailey met at Burleigh. She educated him about every facet of the company and the specific language of pottery making: the fettler, the jolly, the monkey’s tail, the sherd-ruck, the potter’s rot. “I think you were cleaning everything up as well, after everyone had gone,” remembers Bailey. “We do wear a few hats,” says Baskeyfield.

Christopher Bailey at his latest workplace, Middleport Pottery in Stoke-on-Trent.

In a recent development, “Feeling the weight of a 175-year-old company and giving its best face to Christopher when he first visited was a huge responsibility. I gave it a decent stab,” she continues.

“You did more than that,” replies Bailey. “You made me fall completely in love. I called Simon and remarked, ‘We’re putting our pension into a little pottery in Staffordshire.’”.

“I just felt good here. I felt quite nurtured,” he says of his inauguration into the company, as we wander through its endless ateliers. “I grew up in a very post-industrial, historically thriving textile town, and the majority of businesses there were on their last legs.” Here, every employee has a unique skill, something that can only be done by hand. “Once I heard the most beautiful sound, and I was told, ‘Shirley’s listening to the pings.’ She tings the piece she’s working on with another piece of pottery and can tell if there’s any air trapped in it.”.

In a ground floor room is a Dickensian treasure trove of white plaster molds, housed on floor-to-ceiling shelving. “Magical,” is how Bailey describes it. “I need to get everything digitized,” he says with a sigh. Archiving is a substantial future project. “We make things, but there’s never been a pause to say, ‘What do we have? And how can we make sure that we’re protecting things and using things?’ Because right now, it’s quite difficult to… find things. I’ve had quite a few projects where I just need to know, do we have this kind of a shape? This kind of a size? This kind of a vessel? And two days later, I’m still searching for it.”.

The Arden design on this teacup has been part of Burleigh collections for more than 100 years.

They have a collection of more than 25,000 master molds; a complete archive of engravings, which number more than 5,000, from across the organization’s history; and all of the original engraved cylinders. “So, basically, the tissue transfer process is where you get a copper cylinder, you hand-draw the design and then engrave it with a hammer and tools. So you’ve got two rollers and you put tissue through it, along with an ink,” Bailey explains, emphasizing that the only thing that doesn’t come from within 100 miles is the tobacco tissue—the right consistency and weight—from France. “Then these very skilled people cut the printed tissue out, and they literally wrap the vessel, whatever it is, a teapot, a cup, a plate. And with a brush, they push the ink into what’s called biscuit, where the pot has gone through the kiln one time. The paper gets washed off leaving the print, which gets glazed and goes for another firing in the kiln. And that kind of firing changes the color.”.

Bailey had always thought that if he decided to have “another phase of life,” it would be in a big, tech-based—“because I love technology”—fashion company. “And so it’s quite funny that the thing that actually made my heart sing is practically AI-proof, because it can’t be replicated by technology.” He has plans to make the product—which is sought after by Soho House, William Morris gallery, and Ralph Lauren—more eclectic. “We’re very botanical, we’re very flowers and leaves. How can that kind of evolve? The patterns and colors, I think, can continue to have creativity instilled in them.”.

Once fired, items are stored in the biscuit warehouse.

Recent findings suggest that there are similarities between the worlds of fashion and pottery. “I remember, when I was 16, taking a coach to Paris from Halifax because I wanted to get into the Mugler and Chanel indicates,” Bailey recalls. “I was a 16-year-old snotty-nosed kid, not dressed the way that you should be dressed for that kind of audience. I was very naïve, but I found it a magical world. And the way it’s changed, that kind of industrialization of fashion—it’s just what’s happened in much of the ceramics industry.”.

At Burleigh, the hand still sings. “I really feel, in some ways, it’s this extraordinary 175-year-old start-up,” says Bailey, “and I’m enjoying that. I’m enjoying rolling up my sleeves. At Burberry, it was just an enormous responsibility. And I feel that here, but actually, I’m starting at the bottom. My whole mantra is: preserve this, but just make sure that we put in really good systems underneath.”.

According to recent reports, hailing from a working-class background, Bailey views his hard work as a badge of honor. “My parents were grafters and they instilled that in me,” he explains. “But my girls… I stopped working when they were very young. I felt concerned that they were seeing me always being available and my purpose was solely to look after them and our life and our family. Parenting is an incredible skill and something that I’m very much learning. But professionally, I wasn’t really doing anything. And so I feel really excited and kind of slightly relieved that the girls are seeing me doing something that I’m loving. I’m not being paid for it, but that’s OK. One day it might happen.”.

Brushes and tools of the trade.

“I’m working very late at night and very early in the morning—on every facet. The operational side, the team side, the where-to-invest side, the rebuilding a website, the creative voice. I’m feeling energized by it.” He looks around the pottery’s workshops. “The team is really generous,” he adds. “They’re very proud. And so many of the amazing people here, their grandparents and parents were in the potteries. And so it’s not so much a job or a vocation. It is a culture.”.

At the end of the day, when he considers the Burleigh world, “I feel joyful,” claims Bailey.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

A “baecation” often entails a romantic getaway, passionate activities, and a lot of vacation sex. But what if traveling with your significant other meant a lot of difficult conversations, a heated back-and-forth, and working to fix your relationship. I know: this sounds nothing like the dreamy R&R you pictured—but for some couples, it’s exactly what they planned for.

According to Booking.com’s 2027 Travel Predictions, 58 percent of U.S. travelers said they would consider taking a trip to resolve conflicts or arguments.

Now, traveling itself already can cause real strain and arguments on relationships on its own. In the same data set, more than one-third of respondents said they found out they were incompatible with their companion after a trip. Nearly three in 10 people have considered ending a relationship or friendship over a trip, while more than one in five have actually cut a vacation short because of a bad travel companion.

Industry observers note that but if you’re already having relationship challenges with your partner, is a trip a good idea? People still seem to think so. About 81 percent stated that taking part in at least one vacation activity with another person helps them have honest or difficult conversations.

So should you be planning a trip the next time you and your partner start arguing?

A change of scenery might be exactly what you and your partner need to see eye-to-eye again.

“Getting away from work, chores, kids, in-laws, or house and childcare stuff can lower defenses,” couples therapist Justena Kavanagh tells Cosmopolitan.

She explains that when you’re home, you’re essentially having every argument on the same “battleground.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Somewhere fresh often brings back the honeymoon period, when you could really see each other without life’s stresses in the way,” she says. And if both you and your partner have busy lives and packed schedules, a vacation may really be the only time you can focus on the issues in your relationship without distraction.

Plus, vacations encourage you to relax—which can go a long when in an argument. “When we’re rested, we’re more regulated, and when we’re regulated, we can listen instead of defending,” Kavanagh says.

She explains that it’s important to establish why exactly you’re going on the vacation in the first place. Are you getting away to talk about an problem? Or simple to get away from it and reconnect? Agreeing on the purpose for the trip before you start packing your bikini will help you and your partner get on the same page—so you don’t end up just arguing more later.

Industry observers note that “Trips suit conversations about connection, like feeling distant, intimacy, or where the relationship is going,” she says. Other things like finances or in-law conflicts may need a follow-up at home.

Recent findings suggest that if you decide that you’re going to talk your issues out, remember that you are still on vacation. That doesn’t mean everything has to be wonderful, of course. But Kavanagh encourages couples to treat the trip like a summit. This means talking early in the day (after a good night’s rest) and working on things while taking breaks.

The trip should essentially be your opportunity to discuss what’s presently happening in the relationship, where you want the relationship to go, and how to shift priorities to get there.

Sure, a beautiful view and hotel sex will definitely lighten the mood and probably even make you more agreeable—but it isn’t a magical bandaid for your relationship challenges.

“If couples don’t have relational skills at home, they won’t miraculously have them on vacation,” Kavanagh warns.

Industry observers note that so if you’re going to go on a vacation to work on things with your partner, you’re going to want to put a plan into place. The best method? Talking about the pattern behind the argument, rather than hyperfocusing on the latest incident.

And even if you do come to a resolution on vacation, make sure you’re setting a plan in place for the positive energy to flow into your everyday lives.

According to recent reports, “Be realistic about home, where you’re more stressed and old patterns return fast,” Kavanagh says. “Initiative follow-up support, a regular check-in, and what you’ll do when things go off track, because they will.”.

In a recent development, okay, so not all of us can afford to book a flight every time we get into an argument with our partner—but you don’t have to. Out of all the activities that people do on vacation, respondents mentioned that it was mostly hikes or walking that was the most effective at getting them to open up and have the difficult conversations.

Lucky for you, taking a hike is totally free—and can do wonders for whatever problem you may be facing with your partner.

Kavanagh explains that walking and hiking take pressure off of an argument.

According to recent reports, “Face to face can feel like a confrontation; side by side, you’re facing the same direction and don’t have to hold eye contact in the hardest moments,” she explains. This is something we see in psychotherapy: think about someone lying on a couch, looking at the ceiling. This helps physiologically and emotionally. Plus the actual physical activity helps, too.

“Walking also discharges stress and is a natural form of bilateral stimulation, the left-right rhythm used in therapies like EMDR,” she claims.

When your partner is irritating you, it’s likely that the last thing you want to do is travel with them. But if you’re determined to move past whatever may be causing a rift, that might be exactly what you need.

It has been revealed that honeymoons and other happy occasions shouldn’t be the only time we travel with our partners with the purpose of growing closer, reconnecting, and strengthening the relationship. Sometimes, even in hardship, a little getaway could be the jumpstart your relationship needs to get back on track. Just remember that after the vacation ends, you do have to go back to reality.

“The good feelings are real, but the test is whether they last back home, where life is harder,” Kavanagh says.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a substantial, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.).

Recent findings suggest that broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Sources indicate that remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#146402. Nature on the Board: Should Brands Opt In?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2291 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vogue ↗ Open Full Page

Nature on the Board: Should Brands Opt In?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story is part of ‘The Business Case for Nature’, a series exploring fashion’s impact on nature and vice versa.
  • Recent findings suggest that for 50 years, natural beauty company Faith In Nature has been guided by the slogan ‘nature is the boss’.
  • Industry observers note that enter Nature on the Board (NOTB), a growing global movement where companies appoint a proxy for nature to their board of directors, recognizing and advocating for the rights of nature in decision-making processes, and flipping traditional corporate governance on its head.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story is part of ‘The Business Case for Nature’, a series exploring fashion’s impact on nature and vice versa. Read more here.

Recent findings suggest that for 50 years, natural beauty company Faith In Nature has been guided by the slogan ‘nature is the boss’. It was plastered on the office walls and repeated ad nauseam by staff, but had no legal footing. Then, in 2021, creative directors Simeon Rose and Anne Hopkins put the provocation to a group of groundbreaking legal experts: how could they turn the slogan into something more?

Industry observers note that enter Nature on the Board (NOTB), a growing global movement where companies appoint a proxy for nature to their board of directors, recognizing and advocating for the rights of nature in decision-making processes, and flipping traditional corporate governance on its head. Some companies appoint a nature director — a human proxy for nature, who holds a formal board seat, written into the manufacturer’s articles of association, with the same financial and legal duties as other board members. Others appoint nature guardians, who perform a similar role in advocating for nature at the board level, but they don’t necessarily have voting rights.

A new programme by Kering and the Centre for Sustainable Fashion hopes to reimagine how companies make high-level decisions, but is the industry ready to embrace change?

NOTB was proposed by Faith In Nature, and fleshed out by legal non-profits Lawyers for Nature and the Earth Law Center (ELC), but it was inspired by Indigenous communities who have practiced nature-centric governance for millennia. “The current business system is operating exactly as it was designed to: businesses pool capital, build goods and services at scale, speed and low cost, and accrue benefits for shareholders,” explains Mary Johnstone-Louis, senior fellow in management at the University of Oxford’s Saïd Business School. “Putting nature on the board is radical because it introduces a stakeholder on which every business depends, but whose interests are not typically represented at the board level.”.

While there was no precedent for putting nature on the board, there were other case studies to draw on, says Lawyers for Nature co-founder and managing director Brontie Ansell. “Until relatively recently, women were seen as objects of law, rather than subjects of law. Like nature, they were not allowed to hold property, vote or voice concerns. Now, we look back on that with horror,” she explains. “Likewise, we are very familiar with widening the stakeholder pool in boardrooms. Many now include HR managers, union representatives, and health and safety officers. Extending this to nature is critical to human survival.”.

Alongside Faith In Nature, NOTB has since been adopted by dozens of companies, including British interiors brand House of Hackney, Norwegian apparel brand Northern Playground, and French IT services organization Norsys. Each has put their own spin on the blueprint, contributing to a fast-evolving consensus on best practices, and throwing open the doors for further innovation. Vogue Business invited these early adopters to share the tensions, toggles and opportunities.

Businesses are just as diverse and idiosyncratic as nature, says Faith In Nature managing director Hannah Whittaker. When it comes to putting nature on the board, each business has to do it in its own way.

NOTB encourages companies to give nature voting rights, but it’s possible to test nature governance without this. Outdoor apparel brand Patagonia made waves in 2022 when it created a nature purpose trust model, making a collection of environmental non-profits the beneficiary of 98% of its non-voting stock, while retaining approval rights in the Patagonia Purpose Trust, controlled by the family of founder Yvon Chouinard.

According to recent reports, approaches may also differ by jurisdiction, notes ELC’s nature governance business development associate Anna Solgaard, who acts as the nature guardian for Norwegian clothing label Northern Playground. Finding ways to give nature more legal rights requires “creative lawyering”, adds Alexandra Pimor, director of the ELC’s Nature Governance Agency. “That’s the beauty of nature on the board: we did not have to change the law to do it, we just changed our relationship with the law to give it a different purpose [taking existing rights for board members and extending them to nature]. In a capitalist environment, the corporate world is probably the easiest place to embed the voice of nature, because companies are given so much freedom.”.

In a recent development, at Norsys, nature is both a director and a shareholder with a 10% stake in the business. “This is a strong model because it means nature will always be represented on the board, it’s not just one nomination we forget about in three years,” states the tech giant’s nature director Frantz Gault, author of Nature at Work and co-founder of Vivøices, a public interest organization promoting the representation of the living world in organizational governance. Gault helped design the nature governance at Norsys, complementing his own role with a council of advisors, who also decide how dividends from nature’s 10% stake are spent.

Industry observers note that lawyers for Nature, on the other hand, prefers for nature directors to remain as “conflict-free” as possible. In the frameworks it has designed, nature representatives are not heavily salaried by the company, they don’t have a bonus linked to profit, they don’t owe the company money or vice versa, and they don’t have — or at least, they commit to disclosing — any other conflicts of interest. “By minimizing those conflicts, the nature representative can speak in the purest form possible about what nature needs,” says Ansell.

At Northern Playground, the articles of association include a “safety valve” whereby the nature proxy can be relieved of their duties if the organization is approaching bankruptcy, to reduce the risk of them being held personally liable.

Another contention point is whether the nature proxy should have the right to veto strategic decisions, as well as voting on them. “If you get to the point where you need a veto, you’ve already lost,” indicates Dr Juliet Rose, head of development at the British botanical garden and research hub The Eden Project, and nature director at Faith In Nature. “You’re trying to get everybody moving in the same direction, so nobody even suggests something that would require a veto.”.

At Norsys, Gault has the power to veto, but has never activated it. To keep the “nuclear power” in check, he is required to confer with a council of 10 scientific experts before taking a position in board meetings. Still, knowing the veto exists can be persuasive enough. “Everyone knows I have the power to veto, so the other directors listen when I speak, and they work with me to find a consensus.” If a veto isn’t on the cards, companies can implement the right to disagree, and the right to express that disagreement in public, adds Gault, or the right to resign. “These are little legal technicalities, but they help make nature’s voice more meaningful.”.

According to recent reports, whichever approach a company chooses, Vivøices recommends running a year-long pilot before codifying nature’s role or communicating the program to consumers. “You do a pilot, then map the impact and what happened, how it changed the way decisions were made, how it influenced the culture internally, and what it means to really integrate the position of nature,” states co-founder Niels de Fraguier.

Sources indicate that when House of Hackney advertised a directorship “for mother nature and future generations” in 2023, it received over 500 applications — its most popular job listing to date. But finding the right person to represent something as nebulous as nature was no small feat. “We had applications from scientists, teachers, poets and everything in between,” says House of Hackney co-founder Frieda Gormley, author of In the Firm of Nature.

Recent findings suggest that the challenge is finding someone who can bridge economic and ecological realities, notes the University of Oxford’s Johnstone-Louis. “They have to protect the tech giant, and at the same time, they have to speak for nature. That means they have to toggle between immediacy and long-termism; between business as usual and what business could be,” she says. Regardless of their professional background, humility and diplomacy are the key competencies, adds de Fraguier.

Both Faith In Nature and House of Hackney appointed Lawyers for Nature’s Ansell as their inaugural nature director, establishing the legal basis for the role and ironing out any kinks. Her successors have wildly different skill sets: Rose has a background in plant science and ecology, while House of Hackney’s nature director Charmian Love specializes in governance, having co-founded B Lab UK, the organization behind the B Corp certification. Love states her goal is to create tools that make it easier for more diverse nature proxies to step into the role in future, while Rose says her success is defined by how well she empowers staff throughout the organization, so whoever holds the nature directorship is not working alone, or resting solely on their own, inevitably limited, experience.

According to recent reports, ideally, nature-centric decision-making cascades down through the firm, and the nature director works in tandem with a well-established nature lead. While the former stewards the long-term purpose of the business, the latter embeds it in day-to-day operations. Without a nature director in their corner, a nature lead can easily fall into the same trap as sustainability leads, tasked with overhauling the business but lacking the resource or buy-in to do so, instead operating in a silo and trying to shoehorn change into business as usual. And without a nature lead to operationalize nature-centric decision-making, a nature director risks becoming little more than “window dressing”, says Johnstone-Louis.

Industry observers note that to avoid tokenizing nature, Faith In Nature has designed a nature dashboard, which translates its goals into tangible projects each team can track progress against. Projects fall into five governing principles: governance, operational impact, sourcing, community and regeneration. “We had to work through the confusion and connect each team with the outcomes we wanted for nature, each of which has budgets, resources and KPIs attached,” explains Whittaker. “Otherwise, the concept can be quite theoretical for staff.” These projects span from changing the adhesive on labels to make at-home recycling easier, to running the brand’s first major television ad in collaboration with Channel 4 and B Corp.

At House of Hackney, Love starts every board meeting with a nature degradation pulse-check and a poem about nature, based on climate policy leader Nigel Topping’s remarks that “we need to be guided by science and moved by poetry”. Beyond board meetings, Love has defined 10 topics that are material to nature, from supply chain and procurement to regulatory changes and financial investments. Decisions about these topics are automatically escalated to a monthly nature meeting. She has also introduced a spin on the traditional ‘going concern test’ boards use to assess how nature-related decisions will affect the manufacturer’s future viability and license to operate.

In a recent development, on top of this, Love has a private email address where staff can discreetly voice concerns or ideas, and the company regularly invites inspirational nature-related speakers into the office. The next phase is to trial a physical card game, she says, which will live in every meeting room, encouraging staff to question their daily decision-making through a nature-centric lens, inspired by similar games at tea brand Pukka Herbs. And at the end of the year, House of Hackney will publish an open-source toolkit for NOTB, informed by its Greenprint fellowship, where 10 SMEs — including Lush, Davines and Vivobarefoot — experimented with nature governance over 12 months.

NOTB is not just another sustainability box for companies to tick; it’s a paradigm shift that goes beyond sustainability, toward regeneration.

Sources indicate that “Philosophically, these are two very different landscapes,” explains Solgaard. “Sustainability is an anthropocentric paradigm, but nature is ecocentric, which means that the more-than-human world is valued alongside humans. Sustainability works with separation and reductionism, which is why we have all these boxes to tick, and we struggle to view things holistically, or to see how everything is interconnected. Nature is everything.”.

In a recent development, putting nature on the board also means moving beyond the risk mitigation approach that has defined so many corporate nature strategies, and underscored the business case for nature, to date, adds Johnstone-Louis. The risk mitigation approach asks how companies can continue to extract resources like cotton and wool pulp from nature, and reduce supply chain disruption from nature-related disasters like water scarcity and flooding. The NOTB approach — especially for companies like House of Hackney, which have combined nature with future generations — asks how decisions made today will affect the ability of future systems to thrive, sometimes looking as far ahead as seven generations. “It’s a different way of seeing the world,” she adds.

Recent findings suggest that addressing nature directly is a leap into the unknown — not least because so few companies have mapped their nature risks and dependencies. But rather than face this with fear, Pimor encourages companies to see the opportunities. “We are facing the most incredible, unprecedented ecological challenge. Facing the unknown means becoming more open to creativity, innovation and imagination. That’s what the voice of nature brings to the table.”.

Deep transformation tends to be slow and steady, concludes Ansell. “Slow isn’t ideal in the situation we find ourselves in, but it’s better than going backwards. The idea here is for nature to be a gentle guiding voice, moving the rudder one degree at a time until the ship has completely changed course. It’s exciting. There’s so much still up for grabs in terms of distilling the theory and making it work for each individual sector or situation.”.

A good vacation wardrobe starts with what you wear to the airport. Mere days ahead of Thanksgiving, Katy Perry and Justin Trudeau were seen landing in Venice for a little fall getaway. And their outfits were, in many ways, exactly what you’d expect them to be.

For Perry, the flight called for a cozy camel knit set. Towing the line between loungewear and everyday style, the two-piece featured a V-neck sweater with a cropped, boxy silhouette. Drop shoulders gave it an oversize feel, while a pocket at the chest served to elevate the look. The singer wore it with matching pants, designed with a high-waisted fit and loose, relaxed leg. She wrapped herself in a cream scarf for an extra layer and, on her shoulder, carried a black tote with gold hardware.

To further accessorize, the “Teenage Dream” star added narrow tortoiseshell sunglasses, a chocolate-brown Ralph Lauren baseball cap, and some chunky headphones.

Industry observers note that next to her, her boyfriend, the former prime minister of Canada, went for darker hues. He made a statement in a deep-gray crewneck T-shirt that declared he “will yap about books,” and layered up with an eggplant-purple button-up jacket with a pointed collar and chest flap pockets. His dark-khaki trousers finished things off, and he grabbed a trusty backpack for the flight.

Prior to Venice, Perry and Trudeau, who have been romantically linked since the summer of 2025, were seen in Paris and, before that, in Barcelona. While in Spain, the two attended the Metafuturo conference, for which Trudeau spoke about the impact of artificial intelligence alongside Spanish cabinet ministers, business executives, and Olympic athletes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that iam here to debunk a common dating myth: Despite what all the relationship gurus might suggest, dating doesn’t have to be confined to the summer. In fact, some of the best, most romantic dates can happen during the late fall and dead of winter. After all, every street and tree is covered in twinkling lights and the cold weather gives you an excuse (not that you need one) to cozy up next to your crush. Add the festivities of the holiday season on top of all of that and you literally have the makings of a dream date.

Sure, the urge to snuggle up with your coziest blanket and binge your favorite rom-coms is nagging you and your person—I get it. But this holiday season is the time to make your Hallmark movie dreams a reality! Whether you’re looking for an option for a third date with someone you just started seeing or trying to keep things fresh and fun in your long-term relationship, there’s something on this list for you.

Volunteering as a date night is a great way to see someone’s generous side. Find a local donation center, soup kitchen, or a cause that means a lot to you. You’ll be able to tell a lot about your date by their reaction to this idea and how they carry themselves throughout the volunteering.

This one will really test your teamwork. You can either grab a premade kit or go old-school and use a pint-sized milk carton and graham crackers as your base. Some of the premade are pretty simple, while others can be a bit more intricate. Either way, both will force you and your date to work together and problem solve. This will be a good way for those red flags or green flags to show themselves.

Recent findings suggest that because it’s time you get in on the whole matching pajamas and Santa hats. If you don’t want to put out money for a photographer, set up your phone’s camera with a timer and tripod—the photos can look just as amazing!

Elevate your hot chocolate game with fun flavors, like salted caramel, dark chocolate, or peppermint. You can buy premade variety packs or really chef it up with making your own. Whatever you choose, just be sure not to skim on the toppings. Grab marshmallows of all sizes, candy canes, whipped cream (I personally love the boozy vodka-infused peppermint one from Whipshots), and whatever else sounds enticing. You will be chocolate wasted and it will be fantastic.

Recent findings suggest that karaoke isn’t about who sounds the best but who has the best energy. Belt out your favorite holiday jams, from the classics to latest renditions of the season’s most popular songs. It’s truly a perfect way to bond and see if your date can match your vibe.

According to recent reports, this option is such a fun way to spend time together. Whether this is an early date with someone you recently started seeing or an activity you and your longtime love do, it’s great for talking, asking questions, and having fun. If you’re a part of the first group, this can be an opportunity to make a candle for each other—then you could exchange them as a low-stakes holiday gift (because getting a present for your situationship is always tricky).

If you or your date are people who appreciate a good aesthetic, finding a local light show could be the perfect night out. The low lighting and colorful moments can help you draw closer to your person, whether it’s in the car riding through or walking. Light indicates leave room for more intimate conversations to take place, too, if you want that.

In a recent development, the best way to spread holiday cheer is by supporting local businesses. From small batch food to unique clothes and accessories, it’s where you and your partner can shop for each other or grab gifts for loved ones. Oftentimes, these events also have other activities available nearby, like ice skating or photo moments, making for the perfect two-in-one date.

It has been revealed that bring out the creative energy with a cutesy arts and crafts moment. Grab a few blank ornaments, brushes and bottles of paint, stickers, fabric, and whatever else strikes your fancy. Set it all up on a flat surface (like a dining table or floor), throw in a few Christmas songs and snacks, and you’ve got the makings of a simple and fun at-home holiday date night.

In a recent development, speaking of not making date night complicated, a simple stroll through your neighborhood (or perhaps one that’s more festive than yours) can still be made special. Make some boozy hot chocolates or hotty toddies, strap in to all your cold-weather gear, and sidewalk hike through your community. Bonus points for lots of hand holding, hugging, kissing and gossiping about the neighbors inflatable holiday characters in their front yard.

It has been revealed that “Do you want to build a snowman?” Anna from Frozen isn’t the only one who can enjoy the feeling of holiday magic. Similar to ornament decorating and gingerbread house making, building a snowman is the ultimate nostalgia cheat code. While he might not come to life like Olaf, dressing him up with the cutest scarf and hat will still be just as worthwhile.

The intentionality behind handwritten notes will forever show true thoughtfulness. This idea allows the two of you to really get creative with one another and reflect on who in your lives you want to wish a happy holiday season. Whether you’re sending our joint cards or individual ones, let your heartfelt emotions shine through.

According to recent reports, can you technically do this any time of the year? Yes. But walk with me: What makes sporting events special for the holiday season is the amount of on-the-ground activations and curated experiences that teams provide fans. I’m talking seasonal menus galore, holiday-themed lounges, and activations where you can put your partner’s competitive skills to the test. It’s almost like a bunch of dates in one!

In a recent development, warm up from the brisk cool air outside by attending a wine tasting at your local winery or private holiday-themed events. Wines with notes of cocoa, hints of spice, and earthiness are especially great to lean into for rich flavor. They also pair well with heavier meals that people typically enjoy during the winter months.

Love the snow but hate the cold? Search for the nearest igloo dining restaurant near you for a winter lunch or dinner. Usually, the igloos are kind of snug (but not in an uncomfortable way), giving you at-home levels of cozy with a space heater or bonfire. They’re also super festive with the decor, so you and your date will feel all the holiday cheer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

In a recent development, arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

In a recent development, combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

Why Weed Might Actually Be Bad for Your Sleep

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that the study, which was performed by Northwestern University researchers and published in JAMA Network, looked at 1,266 adults who participated in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, which followed participants for 35 years to determine how behavioral, biological, and environmental factors affected their risk of heart disease later in life.
  • Here’s what all of that means: Sleep efficiency is essentially how much of the time you spend in bed you’re actually asleep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everyone’s done it before. A pre-game gummy. A nighttime toke. Weed is, at this point, a widely used sleep aid. It usually works pretty well, too. But if you’ve made it a habit, you might just be sabotaging your shut-eye in the long run. According to a fresh October 2026 study, consuming pot in any form before bed causes people to have poorer quality of sleep—without them even realizing it. In other words: It has exactly the opposite of its intended effect. Here’s what you should know before popping an edible before you doze off.

It has been revealed that the study, which was performed by Northwestern University researchers and published in JAMA Network, looked at 1,266 adults who participated in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, which followed participants for 35 years to determine how behavioral, biological, and environmental factors affected their risk of heart disease later in life. Of that sample size, 891 wore wrist-based activity monitors for at least a week so that researchers could examine their sleep patterns. After analyzing the data, the researchers found that those who were long-term cannabis users had “poorer objective sleep, including lower sleep efficiency, greater fragmentation, and more time awake during the night,” Dr. Thanh-Huyen Vu, an author of the study and a research associate professor of preventive medicine at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, tells GQ.

Here’s what all of that means: Sleep efficiency is essentially how much of the time you spend in bed you’re actually asleep. So, lower sleep efficiency means spending more time lying awake instead of sleeping while sleep fragmentation refers to how often your sleep is interrupted, like when you’re unknowingly tossing and turning to get comfortable. The researchers also looked at how much total time participants spent awake during the night. It all boils down to the fact that long-term cannabis users weren’t sleeping as soundly or as continuously throughout the night—sometimes without them even knowing it.

The researchers can’t say for certain. Because the study was observational, it only established an association between long-term cannabis exposure and poorer sleep quality.

One possibility, Vu suggests, is that cannabis may “alter normal sleep architecture,” potentially changing the way the body cycles through different sleep stages.

Sources indicate that over time, it’s those changes that can contribute to more nighttime awakenings, which result in less restorative sleep. She indicates more research is needed to understand the underlying biological mechanisms.

Deep sleep is one of the most important stages of sleep because it’s the phase when your body recovers physically, processes memory, and regulates the immune system. Interruptions in sleep result in less time during the deep sleep cycle, which inhibits your body from doing all the important things that help you function properly when you’re awake. The less deep sleep you get, the worse you feel in the morning. The reason why participants don’t pick up on these mid-sleep wake-ups is that they’re easy to forget. “Sleep trackers can capture some of these patterns, even when people don’t perceive their sleep as being particularly poor,” Vu says. It’s the same way in which you think you slept eight hours one night but woke up feeling groggy regardless.

According to recent reports, not necessarily. Given the sample population—middle-aged adults—the results may not apply to people in other age ranges or even those who use cannabis for medical reasons. Still, Vu says it’s important for people to understand that cannabis’s relationship with sleep may be more complicated than simply helping you drift off faster.

If you regularly use cannabis before bed, paying attention to your sleep patterns may help you better understand how it’s affecting you. Wearable sleep trackers can offer some insight into nighttime awakenings and sleep efficiency, but you won’t get the same sleep analysis if you were part of a study like this. It might be worth trying out a period where you don’t use weed to fall asleep to see if it makes a difference in whether you feel more well-rested, or your mind feels sharper. Though the study still leaves a lot of questions to be answered, its data is clear enough to make anyone with a nightly gummy habit reconsider.

In the mood to read some Hunger Games books after seeing Sunrise on the Reaping in theaters? Maybe you never visited Panem on the page in the first place. Here’s your guide to how to read Suzanne Collins’s dystopian young adult book series in order. (Remember, even though there are six movies, there are only five books.).

It has been revealed that collins’s trilogy was published in a timely succession back in the day. Then a decade passed, and all of a sudden the author surprised us with a new installment. Are there more Hunger Games books on the horizon? We certainly hope so. But for now, let’s be grateful for what we have.

Recent findings suggest that in the world of young adult fiction, “what if you had to fight to the death with the boy in your class who has a crush on you” is about as perfect as premises get. The emotional stakes are as high as the external stakes. Katniss Everdeen was a survivalist before she volunteered to replace her younger sister in her dystopian society’s televised child slaughter. She could hunt and forage better than most of the people in her Appalachian hometown. What she didn’t know how to do was smile for the cameras and perform for the crowd if that’s what it takes to survive.

Katniss returns to District 12 in a PR relationship with her fellow tribute, victor, and ally Peeta Mellark. They’re miserable on the victory tour, unable to process their feelings and seeing the consequences of their actions everywhere. Then, a year later, President Snow confirms that the third Quarter Quell will be Hunger Games: All Stars. The tributes are all former winners and adults. Are Katniss and Peeta simply back where they started? Not really. This time they have allies, and plans to finally move against the Capitol.

In the final book of the original trilogy, Katniss is being dressed up and manipulated for the cameras yet again. But it’s not the Capitol doing it this time. It’s the rebellion, led by the secret District 13. It’s scary to think about how even if you believe in the cause, you may find yourself using the same methods as your enemy. War has broken out in Panem, and Katniss and Peeta are separated. So much happens in this book that they had to split it into two movies.

According to recent reports, ten years later, Collins returned with a fascinating subject for a new prequel: the 10th Hunger Games, during which a teenaged Coriolanus Snow mentored District 12’s lost victor, Lucy Gray Baird, and fell in love with her while brainstorming how to get the murder reality show better ratings with his classmates. Their romance is not really one that you can root for, because we know we can’t fix him. He had bad vibes all along. But it’s a fascinating, twisted tale of how the Hunger Games as we know it came to be.

Next, of course, Collins answered fandom prayers by writing a Haymitch Abernathy prequel. We now know the story of every single District 12 victor’s games. Background details link District 12 women like Lucy Gray and Maysilee Donner to Katniss Everdeen in fun ways. It also serves as a nice companion to Catching Fire, with many appearances from the victors Katniss and Peeta meet during their own Quarter Quell. But be careful what you wish for, because this is a brutal and bloody book about the many ways the Capitol can edit and control your story using propaganda.

The party line is that Suzanne Collins writes when she is inspired to write, and not a second before. As of the release of the film adaptation of Sunrise on the Reaping, there has not been a newly introduced book announcement. But that hasn’t stopped the theories.

Sources indicate that in the fandom, the character who probably has the most support in this realm is Finnick Odair. He’s sexy, confident, and has a tragically beautiful love story with Annie Cresta, a fellow victor from his district. They were also Career tributes. The districts that chose to buy into the Hunger Games by training children to kill haven’t been explored in depth in the books. There’s definitely potential there for a socially relevant story. What is that process like from the inside? Do they have stage moms? I am all for this, but just have one note: let’s tell it from Annie’s POV.

But there are so many other avenues that a future Hunger Games book could take. Collins could write about Cinna and the world of the stylists. That could include an patch on President Snow’s cousin Tigris. She could leave the games behind and write a book about District 13. (Alma Coin origin story, divas?) What about the unknown, presumably dead victor of the first Quarter Quell? There’s also the Dark Days and the first rebel uprising in Panem. I wouldn’t mind a Plutarch story, as well...but I really think we need to hear from a female character this time.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that alaïa’s designs “were completely shocking” to the public at the time, recounts Laura Camerlengo, curator in charge of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco.
  • Recent findings suggest that born in 1935 in Tunis, Alaïa first trained as a sculptor, a background evident in his body of work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the bandage dress. The zipper dress. The perforated leather. The jersey hoods. The peplummed chemises. Azzedine Alaïa’s designs may not look so radical now, but almost 50 years ago, he changed the collective tide of fashion. The bandage dress is perhaps the most pervasive bit of his legacy, and it is emblematic of how the late French-Tunisian designer ushered in a upcoming body-conscious silhouette in the ’80s, one made possible by technological innovations in materials that sculpted without any rigid, waist-cinching structure.

Industry observers note that alaïa’s designs “were completely shocking” to the public at the time, recounts Laura Camerlengo, curator in charge of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. She has spent the past four years developing a latest exhibition titled “Azzedine Alaïa: Sculpting Fashion,” the first major U.S. retrospective dedicated to the work of the famed couturier. It opened November 21.

Recent findings suggest that born in 1935 in Tunis, Alaïa first trained as a sculptor, a background evident in his body of work. In 1956, he decamped to Paris to pursue fashion full-time. After a brief internship at the house of Christian Dior, he worked under Guy Laroche for less than two years before taking on his own private clients, then launching his own atelier in the late ’70s. From there, he built the house we know today. His obsession with construction and material innovation allowed him to both celebrate and liberate the female form. He passed away in late 2017 at the age of 82.

Camerlengo first encountered Alaïa’s work as an assistant on the “Patrick Kelly Runway of Love” exhibition that the Philadelphia Museum of Art organized in 2014. “I was intrigued by how many of the new designers in Paris at this time were being supported by US consumers and retailers,” she indicates. After ascending to her new position in San Francisco years later, she cold-emailed Olivier Saillard, director of the Azzedine Alaïa Foundation in Paris. He was intrigued, and the two began working together on the exhibition almost immediately.

The exhibition focuses on 80 garments from across Alaïa’s celebrated career, divided over a series of archetypes—the bandage dresses, sculptures and shapes, black and white, silhouettes and suiting, and construction and craftsmanship—to explore how his design aesthetic evolved. Interspersed are designs worn by devotees like Tina Turner, Grace Jones, and Rihanna. One final gallery highlights his personal collections of the work of designers he most admired, like Christian Dior and Charles James.

Ahead, Camerlengo speaks to Bazaar about curating the latest exhibition, contextualizing Alaïa’s work in today’s fashion landscape, and his enduring legacy.

According to recent reports, the exhibition is not chronological. We look at a series of Alaïa’s archetypes like the bandage dress to explore how his design aesthetic evolved over the course of his career. He often himself said that he didn’t want to conform to seasonal trends; he was more interested in the evolution of his designs. And so the gallery indicates a mix of objects dating from the 1980s to his final collection in 2017, and they’re largely grouped by type.

In a recent development, when you come in, you are greeted by Grace Jones, as we say, and the seminal purple hooded bandage dress from the fashion Oscars [a French event held in 1985]. As you move through, you’ll see a selection of the zipper dresses, the chiffon gowns, and other works that tie into some of the other themes. In each space, we mix the time periods. And that was something Alaïa himself often said. [He had a running joke that he didn’t know his own age.] He often said he was “as old as the pharaohs.” Basically, time was a construct for him.

That’s a great word for it. We could think of the popularity of the Japanese fashion designers who obscured women’s bodies with their voluminous styles. We could think of the suiting of the period. The 1970s is this period of workplace equality. Women are wearing suits in the style of masculine dress, but that also means they're obscuring their bodies. And then we can think of pop culture. I always think of Diane Keaton’s Annie Hall in 1977.

Some of the individuals I interviewed for my catalog text who were retailers in San Francisco at the time described Alaïa's designs as being like a whiplash. It was a complete 180 from the styles that they had gotten used to over the past decade, which also includes the rise of T-shirts and jeans for women as a mode of dress.

Sources indicate that so here you have these very sexy, very form-fitting clothes. And part of the Alaïa aesthetic, as I see it, is the reclamation of the gaze. Rather than women being passively looked at—usually by men—they are instead commanding their own agency. As you stated, it was completely earth-shattering and very shocking at the time.

It has been revealed that azzedine Alaïa was one of the few couturiers who could work completely by the methods of tailoring and by draping, start to finish, from the initial concept to the final product. I did not fully appreciate his tailoring and the suits he constructed beforehand. We have a selection of them in a gallery of the exhibition, and their construction is absolutely incredible. The way they fit the body, the way they uplift and empower women through cloth—again, very antithetical to what we saw in the decades prior in the 1970s. These are very form-fitting, tailored at the waist, but they have soft feminine touches as well that give you this interesting mix of femininity and strength at the same time.

It has been revealed that very crucial. We talk in the first gallery about how women, speaking generally, were the architects of his life. He learned to sew from his sister, who was working for a seamstress. He was encouraged by a local midwife in Tunisia to go to school at the Institute of Fine Arts. She helped him forge his papers to read 16—he was only 15 at the time. He learned his skills, not in formal training, but from women in Tunisia.

And then his early work was supported by a lot of leading figures of international society, including various Rothschilds, the French performer Arletty, the Swedish American actress Greta Garbo, and that's all before he even started to work formally under his own label in the 1980s. Of course, in the 1980s, he adopts Naomi Campbell, who becomes his protégé. He has close relationships with Grace Jones and Tina Turner. They were hugely vital to him. In the exhibition, the clear invisible mounts that we use are actually based on the body of Naomi Campbell.

Probably the Grace Jones bandage dress from the fashion Oscars in 1985. Not only is it the progression of the bandage dress style that he experiments with throughout the course of the 1980s, but it represents a key moment in his career where he receives two very high accolades as part of the fashion Oscars and he’s recognized for his genius.

As far as the designs themselves, I think we would consider the bandage dress, for example, an iconic symbol of late 20th- and 21st-century fashion developed by Azzedine Alaïa, but of course iterated upon extensively. We've seen surges and resurgences in its popularity ever since.

And then as far as the landscape of the broader fashion system, Alaïa was someone who really eschewed seasonal calendars and trends. He was unconcerned with making things for the market. He often wanted to just produce clothes and share them when he felt they were ready. So I think his method of working foreshadows some of the conversations we’re having now about the overproduction of fashion and the overconsumption of fashion, even the detrimental environmental impacts that we see connected to it. He was really a forerunner, in a sense, to question the fashion system.

Industry observers note that you can see how he really studied the construction of other garments and then adapted it in his own way in his designs. For example, he admired the work of Charles James, the great American fashion designer who was able to manipulate fabric to achieve weightless volume. And you see in Alaïa's own collections as he continues in his career, he does radial tucks and pleating to also get a certain amount of weightless volume in some of his gowns, very much in the spirit of James.

I hope our visitors appreciate the artistry of his work, first and foremost, and also the importance of handcraftsmanship. We are increasingly in an age of technology, especially with the rise of AI. What he created by his own hand is something that we can really marvel at.

Not only the perfect satin shade of cranberry sauce but a waistband that allows for all the stuffing! —Chloe Malle, head of editorial content.

Should You Worry About That Bump on Your Chest?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if you’re like most guys, you probably have plenty of little bumps and lumps on your skin.
  • While male breast cancer is rare, estimates suggest that more than 2,600 men are diagnosed with an invasive form of the disease each year in the United States, and more than 500 die, according to the American Cancer Society.
  • It has been revealed that there isn’t a universal description of what breast cancer lumps look like in men, but there are some common characteristics to keep in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you’re like most guys, you probably have plenty of little bumps and lumps on your skin. There’s the callus on your toe from training for that 10K, the razor bumps along your neck from this morning’s shave, and the skin tag on your underarm you keep meaning to get removed. While it’s often completely fine to ignore these bumps, that isn’t always the case. Some can be a red flag worth paying attention to—especially if they’re on your chest.

While male breast cancer is rare, estimates suggest that more than 2,600 men are diagnosed with an invasive form of the disease each year in the United States, and more than 500 die, according to the American Cancer Society. And one of its telltale signs is a firm bump under or near your nipple. Below, find out more about what a breast-cancer lump may look like and four other things that could be to blame for a new bump on your chest.

It has been revealed that there isn’t a universal description of what breast cancer lumps look like in men, but there are some common characteristics to keep in mind. “Breast cancer in men typically presents as a painless, firm, or hard lump,” notes Jose Pablo Leone, MD, the director of the Program for Breast Cancer in Men at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

Sources indicate that another sign that the bump could be breast cancer is if it’s behind or very close to the nipple and areola. “Men have much less developed breast glandular tissue than women, which is why breast cancer in men most commonly develops near or behind the nipple,” claims Dr. Leone. As for size even a lump as small as a pea can be cancerous, but by the time men go to the doctor, tumors are often larger than a marble, according to Dr. Leone. “In part because of the lack of awareness and screening, most men present with larger tumors,” he says. “But any size is worth mentioning to your doctor. Not all breast cancers feel the same, so any fresh or persistent breast lump should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.”.

Your chest has a lot of oil glands, which can set the stage for pimples. “Staying in a sweaty shirt after a workout can make chest acne flare, especially if the fabric is tight and rubs against your skin,” says Elizabeth Bahar Houshmand, MD, a board-certified dermatologist based in Dallas. While blackheads and whiteheads are typically small and easy to identify, inflamed pimples or nodules may seem more alarming because they can be hard, painful, and form deep under the skin. When it comes to nodular acne specifically, you can’t treat it on your own. If that’s what you think you’re dealing with, see a dermatologist, who can prescribe an oral or topical medication to help clear it up.

Sources indicate that “This is a collection of fat that forms under the skin,” says Sonya Kenkare, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Illinois Dermatology Institute in Hinsdale, Illinois. “It is usually soft, not painful, and you can move it around in all different directions.” You don’t need to do anything about a lipoma, but if you want to get it removed, you can talk to a doctor about it.

When hair follicles get inflamed or infected, you can end up with folliculitis. “Folliculitis often looks like small pimples or pus-filled bumps centered around a hair follicle” claims Dr. Houshmand. “They may itch or feel tender.”.

In a recent development, blockage or damage to a hair follicle can also cause epidermal inclusion cysts. These cysts occur when dead skin cells get trapped under the surface instead of shedding. “They feel somewhat firm and often have a central little black spot,” says Dr. Kenkare. Sometimes simply applying a warm compress to the area can help a cyst heal on its own, but a doctor can also inject it with a steroid to reduce swelling, drain it, or surgically remove it.

This condition occurs when breast tissue gets enlarged in men, and it can first appear as a lump under your nipple. “It often feels like a rubbery or firm disc beneath the nipple, and it may be tender,” says Dr. Houshmand. While gynecomastia can come on as a side effect of some medications, like antibiotics or antidepressants, or diseases like thyroid disorders, sometimes there is no clear cause at all.

Industry observers note that if you’re starting to feel like it’s difficult to tell on your own what the lump on your chest might be, you’re not wrong. That’s why it’s best to have your primary care physician look at any upcoming, unexplained bumps and tell you whether you need imaging, like a mammogram with an ultrasound. That may sound scary, but it’s really just covering your bases. “Uncommon things are uncommon, and breast cancer in men is uncommon,” claims Dr. Leone. “You shouldn’t worry excessively about male breast cancer, but you should be aware of it.”.

If you’re a fan of The Hunting Wives, chances are you’re probably invested in the on-screen affair between Brittany Snow and Malin Akerman’s characters, Sophie and Margo. But off screen, both actresses are happily in relationships—Akerman with her husband of eight years, Jack Donnelly, and Snow with new fiancé Hunter Moreno.

For the first time, I’m gonna tell you, I’m gonna tell you. Yes, we’re engaged, yeah. I haven’t said it before. It’s okay. It’s not that major of a secret. I mean, like, who cares?”.

Sources indicate that in talking about her husband-to-be, Snow revealed that the two began dating during the filming of the first season of The Hunting Wives. “He’s the best,” she grinned, adding that Akerman was one of the people to encourage the relationship early on.

Akerman, who was also a guest on the show, added, “We all met him. We got to be, like, the first ones to judge him. Like, ‘This is the right energy for you.’”.

The costars then playfully admitted they jokingly refer to the cast’s boyfriends and husbands as “The Hunting Husbands.”.

So, who is Snow’s fiancé, Hunter Moreno? Ahead, everything to know about the creative and their relationship.

Based in Los Angeles, Moreno began his career directing and filming YouTube videos for influencers before expanding into music, directing videos for artists including Dasha, Charlie Puth, Ava Max, and Machine Gun Kelly. Along with his video credentials, he’s also photographed artists from Selena Gomez to Lizzo, Renee Rapp, and Cara Delevingne. Moreno has also shot fashion editorials and campaigns for publications and brands including Vogue and Madewell.

In 2018, Moreno founded Make Sure Your Friends Are Okay (MSYFAO), a mental health awareness organization that sells clothing and merch, with a portion of its proceeds benefiting various mental health charities.

The initiative is rooted in Moreno’s own experiences with mental health. In an Instagram post shared in May, he opened up about his struggles with depression and the personal reason he started the organization. “In 2018 I started Make Sure Your Friends Are Okay for a selfish reason I didn’t say out loud: I hoped someone would check on me while I was struggling with my own mental health concerns and depression,” he wrote. He went on to encourage others to check in on the people they care about and make conversations about mental health more normalized.

Sources indicate that mental health advocacy is also important to Snow, who co-founded September Letters in 2020. The letter-writing platform, which has partnered with the Mental Health Coalition, aims to help end the stigma surrounding mental health.

According to recent reports, moreno and Snow were first publicly linked in October 2024, when they were photographed kissing while walking through Newly introduced York City. During a 2026 appearance on The Drew Barrymore Show, Snow confirmed that the two began dating during the filming of The Hunting Wives’ first season, which began in 2024.

According to recent reports, on March 28, 2026, Snow made their relationship Instagram official—though it was slyly packed into a massive carousel post. Amongst the photos from her birthday celebration in the desert were two photos of Snow and Moreno, a mirror selfie and a photo of the two posing with her dog.

Though Moreno’s Instagram is mostly dedicated to his professional work, in September, he uploaded a carousel of photos taken of Snow while traveling from Italy to France.

Sources indicate that rumors of an engagement first sparked between Snow and Moreno in November 2025, when a video shared by DeuxMoi highlighted Claire Danes chatting with Snow on a red carpet and seemingly congratulating her on her engagement. “You’re engaged?!” Danes exclaimed during the exchange. Nearly a year later, Snow finally confirmed the news during an appearance on The Drew Barrymore Show.

In a recent development, “You know what? For the first time, I’m gonna tell you, I’m gonna tell you. Yes, we’re engaged, yeah,” Snow said when Barrymore asked her directly. “I haven’t said it before. It’s okay. It’s not that big of a secret. I mean, like, who cares?”.

While gushing about her fiancé alongside Barrymore and her Hunting Wives costar Akerman, Snow called Moreno “the best.” She also revealed that Akerman played a role in their love story, encouraging Snow to pursue the relationship early on.

Heated Rivalry caused such a kerfuffle at the end of 2025 that we all collectively as a society forgot that The Hunting Wives got us all hot and bothered with sexy, covert, queer relationships earlier that summer. The Netflix series is now back for season 2 for more deliciously toxic drama. It’s also back with some new characters. Here’s what you need to know about who plays who in The Hunting Wives season 2.

According to recent reports, spoilers for season 1, but unless Katie Lowes and Chrissy Metz’s characters decide to haunt the Hunting Wives in season 2, they won’t be returning. And before we get into the major players, additional new cast members on The Hunting Wives season 2 include Cam Gigandet as Gentle John Moffitt, WNBA player Angel Reese as “Trainer Barbie,” and Casey Mills as Nico.

Brittany Snow plays Sophie O’Neil.

Sources indicate that in the first season, Sophie was a fish out of water after moving from Massachusetts to Texas for her husband’s job. Now, she’s acclimated to Southern living; but her old secrets have been replaced with latest secrets.

It has been revealed that brittany is a former child/teen actress who followed three years on Guiding Light with a main role on American Dreams. She then starred in John Tucker Must Die and played Amber Von Tussle in the movie adaptation of the musical Hairspray. Not long after came Pitch Perfect and its two sequels. You’ve also seen her in X, Someone Great, Crazy Ex-Girlfriend, and The Night Agent.

Malin Åkerman plays Margo Banks.

Margo leads the Hunting Wives, a social group for gun and cocktail-loving women in Texas. She takes Sophie under her wing and seduces her in more ways than one, to the chagrin of some of the other women in the group who feel replaced.

It has been revealed that many would say that Malin broke out in the pre-DCU superhero film Watchmen. But they haven’t seen 27 Dresses, The Proposal, or The Comeback. You may also know her from Dollface, Billions, that one episode of How I Met Your Mother, Trophy Wife, Children’s Hospital, Rock of Ages, and two episodes of Entourage.

Evan Jonigkeit plays Graham O’Neil.

Graham is Sophie’s architect husband.

Evan played the Marvel comics character Toad in X-Men: Days of Future Past. His other film and television credits include Easy, Bone Tomahawk, Frontier, and Whiskey Tango Foxtrot. If you like The Bear and Girls, you need to watch Jonigkeit as Will in the Starz series Sweetbitter.

Dermot Mulroney plays Jed Banks.

Margo’s husband Jed is running for Governor!

It has been revealed that dermot’s romantic comedy fame precedes him. You’ve seen My Best Friend’s Wedding, The Wedding Date, The Family Stone, and Must Love Dogs. He’s also a cellist who has played in the orchestras of several film scores, and played onscreen in Mozart in the Jungle. On television, he had a short arc on Friends and longer recurring roles on demonstrates like Latest Girl and Enlightened. He was a regular on Shameless and plays the main character Dom in the Chicago Fire/Med/PD world.

Brad is the teenage son of a late Hunting Wife named Jill.

Ferrier’s previous credits include Dirty Laundry, Sweet Tooth, and One Of Us Is Lying.

Callie is the sheriff’s wife and Margo’s ex-situationship.

Jaime Ray Newman is set to appear next in the Netflix true crime drama The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey. You also know her from Dopesick, The Magicians, The Punisher, Bates Motel, Wicked City, Drop Dead Diva, Major Crimes, and Veronica Mars. She was also on General Hospital for three years in the 00s.

Hunter Emery and Karen Rodriguez play Deputy Walter Flynn and Deputy Wanda Salazar.

The cops investigating various local crimes that may/may not involve the wives.

Earlier this year, Karen Rodriguez played Janet Ruiz on Spider-Noir. And you know Hunter Emery best as CO Rick Hopper on Orange Is the New Black.

IG: @itsjusthunteremeryIG: @xkarenxrodriguez.
