Kim Matula was a series regular on The Bold and the Beautiful in the 2010s and was nominated for a Daytime Emmy Award in 2014. She was also a series regular on UnREAL and LA to Vegas. She starred alongside Florence Pugh in the underrated gem Fighting With My Family and also played Jane Curtin in Saturday Night.

Alex Fitzalan plays Lincoln Trout.

Lincoln is also a newly introduced character this season.

Alex Fitzalan has, on two separate occasions, been part of a teenage survivalist ensemble series: The Society on Netflix and The Wild on Prime Video. His film credits include 2018’s Slender Man and 2022’s Chevalier. Earlier this year he also turned up on The F Ward and the Netflix adaptation of My Brilliant Career.

Whoever Chase is, he seems fun!

John Stamos is best known for playing Uncle Jesse on Full House and hanging out with the Beach Boys in his spare time. He did also have a main role on General Hospital for years before that. Post-Tanner family, Stamos also starred in ER, Jake in Progress, Grandfathered, Scream Queens, and Massive Shot. He has also starred in four musicals on Broadway, and frequently performs at the Hollywood Bowl.

Dale Dickey plays Zelda Moffitt.

And whoever Zelda is, she seems fierce.

Industry observers note that you saw Dickey earlier this year on Widow’s Bay. She is the kind of working actress who’s in everything. Her previous television credits include My Name is Earl, True Blood, Justified, Vice Principals, Claws, A League of Their Own, and Bookie. On the major screen, you’ve seen her in Winter’s Bone, for which she won an Independent Spirit Award, as well as Super 8, Hell or High Water, Palm Springs, and Princess Protection Program.

Other new cast members this season include Cam Gigandet as Gentle John Moffitt, WNBA player Angel Reese as “Trainer Barbie,” and Casey Mills as Nico.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion.
  • In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

It has been revealed that remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been a moment since a show’s had me more locked in than Phony on Hulu, and with just one more episode left, inquiring minds (me) want to know: WHEN IS SEASON 2? And also crucial: is there even going to be a season 2?

Sources indicate that phony follows high schooler Sonny Cooke, who wakes up in the hospital after a car accident to find that his mom seems...off. For starters, her facial features are ever-so-slightly different—but there’s also the fact that she doesn’t remember their special way of saying “I love you” (three hand squeezes), and the fact that she’s just acting generally weird. Was she swapped out by an imposter? Does Sonny have Capgras syndrome? Is there some sort of alternate reality happening? Hopefully we’ll find out by the end of season 1, but then what? Which brings us to...

Not yet. But given how freely the cast and creators are talking about a second season (and the fact that the show is pretty popular), it seems likely to get a sophomore pickup.

Yes...but it’ll also end on a cliffhanger. Creator Nick Paley told Us Weekly “I’m really excited about the cathartic emotionality of the [season 1] cliffhanger. This thing kicks us into the next story in this world because I don’t like constantly depriving people of information. I want this to feel like it means a lot and it feels very crucial to the characters emotionally. So that cliffhanger does both. Every episode has very big turns at the end. When you’re telling a mystery, it’s really important to show it to people who don’t know.”.

Paley told the Los Angeles Times that Phony Season 2 will feature “a whole fresh story” after the season 1 finale delivers “resolutions and answers.”.

According to recent reports, the majority of Phony Season 1 was filmed from March through May of 2026, and it premiered in October—a pretty short production time. So, if the show follows a similar schedule for season 2 and starts filming this spring, we could be looking at another October premiere.

Recent findings suggest that potentially a LOT. Connie Britton, who plays Ellen, told The Wrap, "I think Nick has this thing laid out through probably five or six seasons. He's so clear about what the story is, and so I would be very surprised if he has doesn't have Season 2 all ready to go.".

Breaking: Apple Juice Bread

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level.
  • Industry observers note that I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal.
  • In a recent development, take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

Industry observers note that I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

In a recent development, take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard.

It has been revealed that mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

It has been revealed that do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It didn’t take long for Prager to start getting noticed in art circles.
  • It has been revealed that prager’s color-saturated works capture cinematic scenes that bring to mind classic Hitchcock films.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that alex Prager was in her cubicle at an internet startup, staring at the endless rows of other desks, when she realized that something was terribly wrong. “The rest of my life flashed in my mind,” she says. She began to cry. “It was like that Talking Heads song: And you may find yourself in a beautiful house / With a beautiful wife / And you may ask yourself, / ‘Well…how did I get here?’” she says. “This was not my life.” Soon after, she attended a show of William Eggleston’s work and left certain that her future was in photography. Within a week, she’d bought a used Nikon N90s camera and darkroom equipment. “I just knew, the way that you know you have a face and you know who you love. I knew from that moment forward what my path was,” she says.

It didn’t take long for Prager to start getting noticed in art circles. And this winter will be one of the most significant seasons of her career, with both a major solo museum show at the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, and an exhibition at the New York gallery Lehmann Maupin. DreamQuil, her first feature film, was released in theaters this fall and will be available to stream in December.

It has been revealed that prager’s color-saturated works capture cinematic scenes that bring to mind classic Hitchcock films. She creates full worlds for her photos, with sets, casts, and impeccable period costumes. Her pieces gained notice with her 2007 show “Polyester” at L.A.’s Robert Berman Gallery. The series showed women, perfectly attired in ’60s-era looks, posed in evocative ways. A heavily made-up girl clutches a Massive Gulp, a flaxen braid thrown over one shoulder; four young women huddle together in swimsuits, a plane flying across the perfect blue sky above. An ominous feeling pervades.

Her work sparkles on the surface but explores something darker underneath. “The first color photograph I took was staged and a play on The Wizard of Oz and death, but it was very colorful and beautiful. I was interested in the way to explore something that felt layered. Underneath it, you find there are very uncomfortable things or darker stories and emotions,” Prager explains.

Recent findings suggest that prager steadily built up a following through a series of gallery indicates, but things changed markedly in 2010 when her work was selected to be shown in the elite “Fresh Photography” exhibit at MoMA. She had her first solo show at the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., three years later. She’s also done work for magazines and brands like Cartier, Disney, and Apple.

It has been revealed that “My work has always been about my personal challenges and things that I’m not really understanding in the world, but I think more and more it becomes less about me and my emotions. That’s probably also me becoming a mother and growing up, but the world has changed,” indicates Prager, whose son Francis is 9. The scale of her work has grown—bigger audiences, more ambitious concepts, a greater ability to stage elaborate photography—but the approach hasn’t. It’s still about the questions she needs answers to.

The idea for DreamQuil came to Prager during the pandemic (she was inspired by a meme that advertised YearQuil, a fictitious product that would allow people to sleep through the misery of 2020), and she wrote the script with her sister, Vanessa Prager. Elizabeth Banks stars as a woman who’s living in a depressing future world where people rarely leave their homes and finds herself dealing with her robot clone.

It has been revealed that opening two major demonstrates within months of the release of her film wasn’t something Prager anticipated—each alone would have been a high point in her career—but she often does her best work amid a frenzy of activity. “I thrive in a bit of chaos,” she says. “I like to try to mold it and wrestle with it and attempt to control it and bend it to my will. It doesn’t always happen exactly the way I want, but it infuses me with inspiration and energy.”.

This story appears in the December 2026/January 2027 concern of ELLE.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a latest personality. Unlike plain noodles, which promptly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

It has been revealed that season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

In a recent development, heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

Recent findings suggest that my holidays were split between regions growing up. We spent Thanksgiving at my dad’s side, and Christmas with my mom’s. With my mom’s Alabama and Texas roots and my dad's Missouri and Kansas roots, that meant that Christmas dinner was a Southern affair and Thanksgiving was a Midwestern feast. Both holiday spreads had a fair amount of overlap of dishes (casseroles galore), but I have to say: A classic Midwest Thanksgiving has a special place in my heart.

What makes a Midwest Thanksgiving, you may ask? All of the classics are present, plus a few surprising favorites that, in my house, no holiday is complete without. We think beyond the turkey, sometimes skip mashed potatoes for a cheesy casserole, and have to be careful not to fill up on all the rolls (butter and honey better be on the table). Ready to celebrate Midwest-style? Here are some recipes that your holiday won’t be complete without:.

In a recent development, made with canned pineapple, pistachio pudding, and Cool Whip, this retro crowd-pleasing dessert “salad” will take you straight back to the ’70s with just one bite. It’s the perfect recipe to throw together if you don’t have a ton of time, but you need to take something to that potluck or family gathering.

Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving is equally about food and football, so this tailgate-inspired stuffing is a no-brainer. Filled with beer cheese sauce and topped with crispy bacon, this twist on the classic holiday side is so irresistible, it’ll be gone long before halftime of that first Thanksgiving Day game.

Pepper Jelly & Cream Cheese Bites.

It takes less than than 5 minutes to pour some pepper jelly over cream cheese and place some crackers around. These bites are slightly more elevated without many more steps. It’s for those that want to feel like they are putting some effort into their appetizer without it being difficult or time-consuming.

Don't be fooled by the name—the only thing deathly about this casserole is how absolutely delicious it is. This cheesy, creamy casserole is a staple at every holiday in my Kansas home, and Thanksgiving is no exception. Yes, we often have mashed potatoes too.

Recent findings suggest that for this recipe, we ditched canned cream of mushroom soup and went for fresh instead. It's not how my mom makes it, but trust me—by sautéing mushrooms with sliced onion in butter, you're building a base with some serious depth of flavor. Cook the mushrooms enough that they get a little caramelized, and you'll really be good to go.

Get the Green Bean Casserole recipe.

No matter the holiday, one thing is for sure: Deviled eggs will be making an appearance. Variations are always welcome (looking at you, harissa deviled eggs), but if grandpa is going to have a happy Thanksgiving, then this classic recipe better be present.

Get the Classic Deviled Eggs recipe.

Strawberry pretzel tart, AKA strawberry pretzel salad, might sound a little strange, but trust us—it strikes the perfect balance of whimsical and classic, sweet and salty. The pretzel crust proves to be an ideal complement to the rich cream cheese layer and the sweet strawberries with their Jell-O glaze.

Turkey usually rules the roost at Thanksgiving, but it's not the only centerpiece present at many Midwestern holiday tables. Depending on how many family members are coming, my family has been known to prepare a turkey and a ham—it's the best of both worlds!

According to recent reports, we’re certainly not opposed to roasted Brussels sprouts, but we also love giving them the traditional Thanksgiving treatment—plenty of butter, cream, and cheese. This method upgrades even the most humble vegetables while still allowing them to be the star of the show.

Sources indicate that essentially, this is chicken Alfredo, but with a few extra decadent add-ins, like cream cheese, garlic, and punchy spices like nutmeg and black pepper. When you’re craving the classic but have to serve a crowd, this is the recipe you should make.

In a recent development, A cheese ball is peak party appetizer nostalgia, and these cheese ball bites are here to put a upcoming, shareable twist on the classic. They’re so simple to make, only require a handful of ingredients, and are super versatile based on what you have on hand.

I'll clarify that when I say stuffing, I'm actually referring to dressing. Traditional stuffing should be stuffed inside the turkey and cooked in there, but in my family, we've always called it stuffing. By cooking your stuffing in a baking dish, you get crunchy, buttery pieces of bread on top and soft, bread pudding-esque pieces underneath.

What’s the best kind of potato? A loaded baked potato, of course. With this in mind, we combined the two superstar spuds into one glorious dish. Sweet Potato Casserole With Marshmallows.

If you’re not into creamy, melty macaroni and cheese with a wildly satisfying cheese-pull, then you might want to find another mac recipe. Sorry, but this slow-cooker macaroni and cheese is just too darn dreamy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Industry observers note that note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, swiftly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

According to recent reports, scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In my previous chicken sandwich showdown, I put KFC and Popeyes head-to-head to see which chain served the better sandwich.
  • Recent findings suggest that chick-fil-A has built its reputation around a simple, flavorful chicken sandwich that doesn’t need much to stand out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Few fast food rivalries are as competitive as the battle for the best chicken sandwich. And while plenty of chains have introduced their own versions over the years, Chick-fil-A and Popeyes remain two of the biggest names in the conversation.

In my previous chicken sandwich showdown, I put KFC and Popeyes head-to-head to see which chain served the better sandwich. Popeyes ultimately came out on top, thanks to its bold seasoning, crispy breading, and well-balanced toppings. This time, I’m putting Popeyes up against one of its biggest competitors: Chick-fil-A.

Recent findings suggest that chick-fil-A has built its reputation around a simple, flavorful chicken sandwich that doesn’t need much to stand out. Popeyes, meanwhile, practically broke the internet when it introduced its now-famous chicken sandwich in 2019, sparking a fast food frenzy.

I ordered each chain’s original chicken sandwich to compare flavor, texture, juiciness, and overall balance. Both have their strengths, but only one can move on as my favorite.

Chick-fil-A’s Original Chicken Sandwich keeps things simple with a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, and a toasted bun.

Chick-fil-A’s chicken is so recognizable for a reason. The seasoning and brine give the fillet a savory, slightly tangy flavor that’s hard to beat, while the crispy breading contrasts nicely with the juicy chicken. The pickles also do their job, adding just enough acidity and crunch to balance out the richness.

My biggest complaint is that I wanted a little more from the sandwich. Compared to other fast food chicken sandwiches I’ve tried, many of which come with some type of sauce, Chick-fil-A’s original feels a bit plain. The chicken has enough flavor to stand on its own, but I think a little mayo or another sauce would have made the overall sandwich even better.

Still, there’s something to be noted for a chicken sandwich that relies almost entirely on the quality and flavor of the chicken itself.

According to recent reports, popeyes’ Classic Chicken Sandwich features a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, mayo, and a toasted brioche bun. The sandwich that practically broke the internet when it launched in 2019 still lives up to the hype.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve had this sandwich before where the chicken was slightly dry in spots, but thankfully that wasn’t the case this time. The fillet was juicy, flavorful, and incredibly well-seasoned. The breading had a satisfying crunch, and the bold, savory flavor made me want to keep going back for another bite.

Recent findings suggest that the mayo was another important part of the sandwich, adding a tangy creaminess that complemented the chicken without overpowering it. Paired with the crisp pickles, it helped balance out the richness of the fried fillet.

In a recent development, I also really appreciated the proportions. The soft brioche bun held everything together without overwhelming the chicken, and each bite had a good balance of meat, breading, sauce, and pickles.

Industry observers note that while Popeyes might not always deliver the most consistently juicy chicken, everything came together particularly well during this taste test. Between the seasoning, crispy breading, and well-balanced toppings, it’s easy to understand why this sandwich became such a phenomenon in the first place.

Popeyes already managed to beat KFC in my previous comparison, and after going up against Chick-fil-A, it’s keeping its winning streak alive.

According to recent reports, chick-fil-A arguably has the more distinctive chicken flavor, thanks to its savory, slightly tangy seasoning. But when I’m ordering a chicken sandwich, I want the entire thing to work together, and that’s where Popeyes has the advantage.

Chick-fil-A is still a great option, especially if you prefer a simpler sandwich that lets the chicken do most of the work. But after trying both, Popeyes delivered the better overall experience. With two wins under its belt, Popeyes is proving to be a pretty tough sandwich to beat.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It’s been living rent-free in my mind for the better part of this year: Conner Ives’s silk brocade opera coat, which captured nearly every fashion lover’s heart when it debuted on the fall/winter 2026 runway at London Fashion Week. Reminiscent of Mary-Kate Olsen’s fur-trimmed Balmain coat from the 2013 Met Gala, this particular stunner, along with the designer’s other iterations, seems to be what every It girl is wearing.

The coat—crafted with silk tapestries dating back to the Qing dynasty and with hand-embroidered depictions of red-crowned cranes, bamboo leaves, and flowers—was undoubtedly the first wave in what would become a tsunami of a trend: opera coats. And while plenty of faux fur-trimmed coats have made their way onto the market, those featuring Chinese imagery like that on Ives’s iterations have taken center stage.

“There’s been a real change in how people perceive Chinese design,” Cheryl Leung, founder and creative director of Sau Lee, tells ELLE. Leung attributes the opera coat’s rise in popularity to fashion’s shift away from minimalism and consumers’ growing appetite for expressive pieces, richer fabrics, and textures. “Brocade is a great example because it has so much character,” she says. “The fabrics can be quite ornate, but when you put them into a modern silhouette or style them with something very simple, they feel completely different.”.

Industry observers note that chinese design has often been presented through a Western lens, but designers like Leung and Kim Shui are creating work rooted in their own cultural perspectives. Shui, the Chinese-American, New York-based creative director behind her eponymous label, has long been drawn to Chinese garments and the ways they communicate identity. “I’m particularly interested in the visual language and craftsmanship of traditional Chinese garments, whether it’s the silhouette of the qipao (a traditional Chinese dress dating back to the Qing dynasty), the richness of brocade, or traditional techniques like embroidery and intricate knot closures,” Shui tells ELLE. “I look at these elements not as things to reproduce literally, but as a vocabulary that I can reinterpret.”.

In a recent development, while the trend has gained widespread popularity, the Chinese design details behind it can sometimes be overlooked. “I’ve seen so many ‘trending winter coat’ videos featuring Chinese brocade coats with fur trim and traditional Chinese embroidered silk coats, but they don’t make any reference to their Chinese origins,” Shui claims. “Instead of using terms like ‘qipao’ or ‘mandarin collar,’ creators will often describe these details generically as a ‘stand collar’ or ‘high neckline.’ It’s important to acknowledge where these design elements come from and the history behind them—why erase the cultural context?”.

Industry observers note that leung sees the coat’s popularity as an opportunity to bring attention to its history and the designers reinterpreting it. Shui and her team have also been creating content about the histories of brocade, embroidery, and the qipao, as well as the cultural references behind her collections to bring more awareness of the craft to her audience.

It has been revealed that “I do think there’s a difference between appreciating a design tradition and overlooking where it came from,” Leung says. “If a designer has been inspired by Chinese textiles, craftsmanship, or traditional clothing, acknowledging that doesn’t take anything away from their creativity. If anything, it gives the work more depth and helps people appreciate the original references.” Shui adds that brands outside the culture have a “responsibility to acknowledge their origins rather than presenting them as an entirely upcoming aesthetic.”.

Industry observers note that fashion has been both a vehicle for cultural exchange and a product of it—and trends will undoubtedly come and go. Not everyone will be interested in the cultural history of the piece they buy—and Leung doesn’t necessarily think they need to be. Shui is happy to see people from all backgrounds embrace garments from outside of their own cultures. “I hope this renewed interest encourages people to look beyond the garment itself and discover the rich traditions and craftsmanship behind it,” she notes.

The morning after Vogue World 2026: Milano, all anyone online wanted to talk about was “the robots”. The moment became a lightning rod for memes, TikTok reactions, and questions about the state of creativity today. It turns out that was sort of the point.

Sources indicate that A couple of months after the event, Anna Wintour, chief content officer at Condé Nast and global editorial director of Vogue, invited Burberry’s chief creative officer Daniel Lee to Upcoming York for a fireside chat at the Vogue Business Global Summit. Lee also wanted to talk about “the robots.”.

A robot walks the runway during Vogue World: Milano 2026.

In a recent development, of course, the two discussed much more than that, taking turns interviewing each other about Lee’s journey at the British brand during a firm-wide turnaround, Wintour’s first job in fashion, the US midterms that happened the day before, and success — spoiler: social media makes it look easy. Ahead of the official announcement, Wintour also teased the Met Costume Institute’s theme for 2027: extraORDINARY.

Sources indicate that anna Wintour: Daniel, good morning. Thank you for coming all the way from London. So Daniel, you chose a very quiet news day here in the US. Have you been following the election news?

According to recent reports, daniel Lee: Yeah, definitely. I was super jet-lagged, so I was watching the news all night.

AW: I have to ask you, how do you think [Senator-elect] James Talarico would look in a Burberry suit?

DL: Well, I’d be happy to see anyone looking great in a Burberry suit.

Anna and Daniel on stage at the Vogue Business Global Summit.

AW: Very diplomatic. I guess you’re a Burberry ambassador. I read that you first thought you wanted to be a designer when your aunt took you to see the windows at Harvey Nichols in Leeds as a boy. I guess the equivalent over here would be Saks. Do you agree?

Recent findings suggest that DL: Yes, I’m afraid that is true. You know, I didn’t fall into fashion by looking through pages of Vogue. That’s probably the story I should start saying. I mean, I grew up in the north of England in an area called Yorkshire, which is very beautiful — it’s in the countryside and very green. It rains a lot.

DL: David Hockney is from my hometown. Also, Christopher Bailey is from the same area [Yorkshire]. The Burberry trench coats are made in that area, so I guess Burberry was somehow ingrained in me since I was born. Clothes were really practical in my childhood. Fashion wasn’t something that was really part of my family or my upbringing. We wore clothes to stay warm and dry.

In a recent development, DL: Very Burberry. As kids, we liked to play outside. We would spend our childhood riding bikes in the rain, in Wellington boots. When Harvey Nichols opened in Leeds, I remember going past that store and seeing these incredible windows, and I guess I realized clothes could be so much more. It was like seeing a fantasyland. I guess that’s when I started to think this maybe could be a career for me.

AW: So did you go to fashion school?

DL: Eventually, yes. As a child, I think my first instinct was to get out of Yorkshire. As much as I love the countryside, I knew there was more. I was curious.

AW: Well, you did just buy a house there, so you must like it?

DL: You stay connected to your roots. But I think, as a 12-year-old, I went to London for the first time, and I remember seeing the variety of people in the streets, seeing the theater, so many things going on. I really wanted to be part of that culture. I think that’s what initially drew me to London and eventually to art school. I went to [Central] Saint Martins. I did an art foundation year, into fashion qualifications later on.

In a recent development, AW: OK. You’re meant to ask me a question now.

DL: Anna, what was your first job in fashion? And what did you learn from it?

In a recent development, AW: I’m going to talk about the first job that I actually enjoyed in fashion, which was working at Harper’s & Queen (now Harper’s Bazaar UK) in London, where there were two to three people — on a good day — in the fashion department. So I went in there, and I was immediately an editor, even though I had zero experience. I was always so very grateful for that training because there were no budgets. I do remember my boss once giving me maybe £10 or £20 and saying, ‘Anna, go to Morocco or go south. Find a sheikh, find a maharaja, and do a shoot.’ And somehow you did. It was just a different attitude. You had to be so creative and make things out of nothing. Because there were no teams at Harper’s & Queen, I learned how to do everything: you covered the market, you did the shoots, you wrote the captions.

According to recent reports, when I came to Upcoming York, I went to work at Harper’s Bazaar [US]. I got fired fairly immediately because they told me I would never understand the American market, which is probably true. I then landed on my feet at New York Magazine, which was unbelievable training because I was working in a newsroom with guys like Nick Pileggi and Tom Wolfe — all the great writers of that time. They didn’t give a damn about what I did. They put me next to the bathrooms, so I got to see everybody coming in and out. Because nobody cared about fashion or style, they just left me alone. Eventually, I got a call from Condé Nast. It’s interesting when you talk to young people today how they’re focused on success, and they’re not focused on learning. Without the base, you can't succeed.

I’m meant to ask you a question now. So, congratulations on your very successful show in September. I think it was the first time you collaborated with anyone creatively, and the person that you chose to collaborate with is Celia Birtwell — she’s an 85-year-old legend in textile design, a partner to the great Ossie Clark. Did you have to do much convincing to get her involved? Maybe explain to our audience a little bit more about who she is.

DL: I would say Celia is probably mostly known as Ossie Clark’s collaborator in all those years of incredible dresses and work that I think is on every designer’s moodboard. And she was also very, very close friends with David Hockney and is a subject in many beautiful pieces of his work. We were celebrating 170 years of Burberry this year. We wanted to do the brand justice, and we were thinking of ways to do new things. I met with Celia, actually, just for a conversation. You never really know if someone’s going to be interested in working together. People are terrified by our timelines.

Textile designer Celia Birtwell with her partner and collaborator Ossie Clark in July 1971. Birtwell’s prints for Clark’s dresses are, in Daniel Lee’s words, “on every designer's moodboard.”.

She came to the meeting saying, ‘You know, I’m really inspired by the check. I love the way Hockney paints ginghams on a tablecloth, the perspective that he gives to that.’ I said, ‘Well, would you be up for making some new work?’ And she did. She started with the checks, then the ginghams, and then the beautiful kind of English florals. Hockney gives me so much joy, emotion and warmth.

Birtwell’s new take on the brand’s check was inspired by the way David Hockney paints gingham on a tablecloth.

AW: Yeah, and he was so prolific, painting right up until the end, using an iPad, using different ways to make art. I’m sure you saw that last incredible show that was on at the Louis Vuitton Foundation in Paris. What a life. [Now] you’re meant to ask me….

Recent findings suggest that DL: Congratulations on Vogue World: Milan. Would you like to talk about the robots?

Sources indicate that AW: I’d love to. So the subject of Vogue World: Milan was our belief in the art of the human hand, the creativity of the hand, and the human mind in the age of technology. And we felt that to add something that represented technology, in a way that was — in my view — faintly ridiculous, reinforced the idea behind the theme of the exhibition. As is often in my case, not everyone agreed with me, but it certainly caused a lot of conversation.

Gigi Hadid at Vogue World: Milano. The show celebrated, in Anna Wintour’s words, “the art of the human hand” in the age of technology.

It has been revealed that we’re moving on now to San Francisco in September, and we’re really going to be addressing the diversity and the incredible communities that live in San Francisco, and how it’s a city that has stood up for so much. The symphony and the museums there are extraordinary.

Recent findings suggest that talking about San Francisco, let’s talk about tech. Your last collection seemed to us that you were really advocating the celebration of imperfection and the romance of things made by hand. Is that true? And what do you feel about AI in terms of your creative work?

It has been revealed that DL: As a child, I would spend my time making birthday cards, making cakes with my mom and making dance costumes for my sister. I’m a maker. Obviously I have a mobile phone, but tech is not a huge part of my life per se. I’m not a substantial computer gamer; I never even check email. I only really use WhatsApp.

Sources indicate that DL: I think that’s what I love about luxury fashion. I really think luxury is about preservation of this savoir-faire, this craftsmanship. One of the main roles of the creative directors and companies today is to preserve that know-how and make it relevant, so that customers today can appreciate it.

OK, Anna, could you tell us more about next year’s Costume Institute show?

AW: Absolutely. It’s going to be extraordinary.

Daniel, I think it’s five years that you’ve been at Burberry?

AW: You went into a company that was in disarray, and looking at it from the outside, maybe not very well run. Two years ago, CEO Joshua Schulman came in. That must have been very welcome to have a good partner. He’s been integral — led by your creativity — to Burberry’s unbelievable turnaround. What is it like to work with Josh?

DL: Josh brought an incredible energy, passion, and belief in Burberry. He loves the brand, and his energy really reverberates in the company. I think that’s the role of a great leader. Josh brought a lot of discipline to the brand. He really grew up in American department stores; he intimately understands wholesalers and has very personal relationships with them.

Recent findings suggest that daniel Lee, Anna Wintour and Burberry CEO Joshua Schulman. Lee credits Schulman, who joined two years ago, with bringing “discipline” and a clear pricing strategy to the brand’s turnaround.

AW: I remember being in your store on a Saturday morning looking for something for a small child, and he was there, folding the scarves.

In a recent development, DL: We laugh, but Josh spends his vacations in malls. We had an executive dinner and were asked about our favorite places, and I’m sure he mentioned a mall in California. When he arrived, he brought a very clear idea around price architecture.

Anna, what do you think the British fashion industry needs at the moment?

AW: I think they need to really focus on who they are. We all look to London for creativity and individuality — and a degree of eccentricity. There’s a freedom to the way you see the kids dressed in the streets there that is the antithesis of American or cool Italian, more luxury dressing. It’s a little bit closer to what I was saying when I first was working in London, when you had to do everything.

Industry observers note that I think that the British Fashion Council really needs to focus on that and make more noise about what you can see in London that you cannot see anywhere else. They have a great brand like Burberry, and it was so wonderful to see McQueen back in London and Christopher Kane at Mulberry.

Industry observers note that they have so many creative kids, students, who can’t get jobs there, so they need to make sure that London becomes more of a global fashion mecca — that the retailers, the CEOs, and the journalists go. [Prime Minister] Andy Burnham seems like he’s going to be much more open to business in the UK, and they need to lean on what they own.

Burberry Spring/Summer 2027, a collection that celebrates handcraft and the brand’s 170th year.

So, the last shows were followed by quite a few creative director departures and appointments. How do you see this constant creative shuffle shaping the industry?

DL: My experience is that it takes time to understand and have a dialogue with the firm that you work for, understand the archive, the culture, the people. It also takes time to build a team, and people need stability. I advocate for continuity. Also, when there are constant aesthetic shifts, it’s hard for the customer to understand that. I think there are moments where things do need to be revolutionized, and change is needed. Change is good. But too much change is discombobulating. It’s incredibly hard when you join a brand.

What do you think is the future of what we used to call magazines?

AW: I was doing an interview with Grace Coddington, who’s worked at Vogue for so many years, and we were reminiscing about when we were only working on print. She was able to go off to these extraordinary locations for what seems like an unthinkable amount of time — probably only with £20 in her pocket. She would go to Scotland for 10 days; she would go to China for two weeks. There was a great luxury in being able to have time to proposal and think about what an problem of Vogue should look like. But it was a very narrow audience. When I first arrived at Vogue, people would disappear in the afternoons because they were going to Jones Beach — there just wasn’t that much to do.

Anna Wintour and Grace Coddington. Recalling their print days, Wintour remembers when Coddington could spend 10 days shooting in Scotland or two weeks in China. That was “a great luxury,” she says, but for a much narrower audience.

Recent findings suggest that how lucky are we now to have all these amazing platforms to talk to our audiences? Our audiences have grown to unthinkable numbers. One of the great experiences and joys of what I do now is helping Adam [Baidawi, GQ’s global editorial director], Chloe [Malle, American Vogue’s head of editorial content], and Chioma [Nnadi, British Vogue’s head of editorial content], and all the editors that I work with over the world.

This afternoon, I’m leaving for Asia to work with our editors in Japan, China, Taiwan, and beyond. And I learn a lot from all of them. You have to be on the ground. I really feel that it’s so important to understand different cultures and how they think and work. I remember years and years ago, when I was first starting out, a great friend of mine stated, ‘Anna, wherever you are, you have to walk in the street, climb a high point, visit a museum, and have a cup of coffee.’ I always remember that. I think sometimes when people get successful, they don’t walk in the street. When you walk in the street, that’s when you see the world.

What advice do you give those who want to become creative directors? Do you think social media has distorted the way young creatives see their trajectory by making them think they can be their own boss, or do you think it’s a good thing?

Sources indicate that DL: I think social media makes things look very easy. People don’t always see the journey: the highs, the lows, the learnings. I don’t think you should set out to be an overnight success or to have instant gratification on social media. I’ve been every level, every part of a studio. I’ve been the intern, the pattern maker, the design director. I’ve lived all those jobs, and I’ve had those experiences, and that helps me do the job I do today.

AW: This is an audience of mostly executives. What’s one piece of advice you would give to them when it comes to working with creative teams?

Sources indicate that DL: I think empathy is very notable, respect is very important, understanding is important, and humility. No one’s right all the time. My favorite kind of working relationship is when it feels collaborative. I think as a creative leader, I try to create a space and framework to allow people to feel safe. I think this is something I once heard you say: ‘You hire great people, and you let them work.’ Trust is important.

  • It has been revealed that it primarily comes down to the crust.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A handful of things are non-negotiable at Thanksgiving. You need turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, and, of course, a slice of pie to round out your meal. And pumpkin pie is the undeniable star of the dessert table.

According to recent reports, but sometimes you're strapped for time and have too much on your plate (pun intended) to whip something up from scratch. So we tried six different grocery store pumpkin pies to find the best store-bought shortcut. And our team's verdict was pretty unanimous, even if it’s a bit hard to hear: No premade pie will ever taste as good as a homemade one.

It has been revealed that it primarily comes down to the crust. Frozen and pre-baked pies typically rely on vegetable-based fat instead of butter because they’re more affordable, reliable, and shelf-stable—but that comes at a cost. You not only miss out on the decadent, buttery taste, but the crusts can also leave an unpleasant film on your tongue.

That said, when you need to outsource to the grocery store, we found two options that will work in a pinch.

The pie that we’d feel most confident bringing to Thanksgiving dinner comes straight from the Whole Foods bakery department. That’s not to say it’s perfect, though. The crust is almost upsettingly pale, but it’s made with real butter and only a little bit of palm oil. And since it doesn’t leave a noticeable film and still lets the butter flavor shine, we’ll let this one slide.

It has been revealed that once you look past the crust’s color, this pie is solid overall. The filling is decadent, not too sweet, and creamy without being mushy. Whole Foods doesn’t shy away from the spices, either.

Senior Editor Samantha MacAvoy noted that the warming spices are nicely balanced, while Designer Alison Dominguez noted, “The flavor was exactly how a pumpkin pie should taste.”.

Industry observers note that costco’s pumpkin pie isn’t perfect: The crust uses palm oil-based shortening rather than butter and can develop a soggy bottom if you buy it too far in advance. (And it doesn’t hold a candle to the warehouse’s holy grail pumpkin cheesecake.) But it has a cult following for a reason, and not just because of its $5.99 price tag.

Even with its faults, the crust has great flavor and enough salt to create a balanced bite. Dominguez appreciated how it was “flaky and not too thick, and most importantly, it let the pie filling itself shine.” News and Features Editor Amanda Mactas chose Costco’s pie as her number one pick. “It all seemed to melt together in one creamy bite,” she said.

And at over three pounds, this dessert is the indisputable champion if you want to feed a crowd for less.

#146349. 8 Reasons to Eat More Oatmeal

📅 17 Apr 2025 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1110 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vogue ↗ Open Full Page

8 Reasons to Eat More Oatmeal

📅 17 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1110 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the humble oat is having something of a wellness renaissance.
  • Dubbed “nature’s Ozempic” on social media right now, oats are enjoying a surge in popularity as interest in GLP-1 medications influences how we shop and eat.
  • It has been revealed that “I eat oatmeal every day,” notes dermatologist and nutritionist Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the humble oat is having something of a wellness renaissance. And while oatmeal may not be the most glamorous of breakfast foods, it’s definitely one of the healthiest. There’s a reason, after all, that oats have been eaten for thousands of years.

Dubbed “nature’s Ozempic” on social media right now, oats are enjoying a surge in popularity as interest in GLP-1 medications influences how we shop and eat. According to a latest report from British supermarket Waitrose, as reported by The Guardian, sales of its Scottish oats have increased by 124% this year. There’s also the rise of so-called “fiber math”—the practice of incorporating more fiber into everyday meals through additions like chia seeds, nuts, and berries. And while no food can replicate the effects of prescription GLP-1 medications, oats are naturally rich in beta-glucan, a soluble fiber that supports gut health and helps us feel fuller for longer. Consider it a newfound appreciation for an age-old breakfast staple.

It has been revealed that “I eat oatmeal every day,” notes dermatologist and nutritionist Dr. Christian Merkel of the Skin and Laser Center in Munich, Germany. “For me, they are a real superfood—and totally underrated.” He notes that not only is oatmeal good for digestion—a key factor in overall health—but it also provides long-lasting feelings of satiety. Below, six reasons why oatmeal should be a regular star in your morning line-up.

“Oatmeal contains a large amount of fiber, which makes it very good for healthy digestion,” notes Merkel. Oats contain both soluble and insoluble fiber: The former, most notably beta-glucan, absorbs water to form a gel-like substance in the digestive tract, while the latter helps add bulk to stools and promotes regular bowel movements. A half cup of dry rolled oats provides around four grams of fiber—a good head start on your recommended daily intake. To further boost the fiber content of your breakfast, try adding ground flaxseeds, chia seeds, raspberries, or chopped almonds. And remember to drink plenty of water throughout the day to help all that fiber do its job.

In a recent development, oatmeal is a good source of vitamin K, which is essential for bone health and blood clotting. It also contains B vitamins—especially B1 (thiamine) and B5 (pantothenic acid)—which are essential for converting protein, carbohydrates, and fats into energy, supporting the digestive tract, making red blood cells, producing hormones, and for healthy skin and eyes.

“Studies have shown that oatmeal has been proven to lower cholesterol levels and can therefore also be beneficial against cardiovascular disease,” indicates Melker, noting that this is also thanks to beta-glucan, the soluble fiber in oats.

In a recent development, oatmeal contains essential minerals such as copper, zinc, calcium, and potassium. It’s also rich in magnesium—crucial for energy, sleep, muscles, protein formation, the nervous system, genes, and more—and is especially high in the inflammation-reducing trace mineral manganese.

Oats are a great plant-based source of protein. “If you compare the nutritional values of different types of grains, you will find that the values of oatmeal are excellent,” says Merkel, noting that this helps balance out the carbohydrates. “The protein content is very good at 5.3 grams per half cup.”.

Though some glucose-experts disagree, Merkel states oatmeal is a safe option for those wishing to keep their blood sugar in check. “There is virtually no sugar in oatmeal which means that your insulin level will not rise quickly when you eat oatmeal,” he says. “Instead, there is a very slight, healthy rise in blood sugar and therefore long-lasting satiety.” Additionally, oats have been shown to lower blood sugar levels—especially in people with obesity or who have type 2 diabetes—thanks to good ol’ beta-glucan’s ability to slow the emptying of the stomach.

According to recent reports, oats have something of an edge over other grains when it comes to antioxidants. They contain a distinctive group of naturally occurring plant compounds called avenanthramides, which researchers have identified as having antioxidant and potential anti-inflammatory properties. While more research is needed to understand their effects on human health, they offer another reason to appreciate the nutritional complexity of the humble oat. For an extra hit of antioxidants at breakfast, top your oatmeal with blueberries, raspberries, or a sprinkling of cinnamon.

Your morning bowl of oatmeal is also breakfast for the beneficial bacteria in your gut. The fiber in oats acts as a prebiotic, feeding gut bacteria that, in turn, produce compounds called short-chain fatty acids. These play an vital role in maintaining the intestinal barrier and supporting immune function. A study published in 2026 in Nature Communications also explored how interactions between oats and the gut microbiome may contribute to their cholesterol-lowering effects. To make your morning oatmeal even more gut-friendly, try adding a spoonful of live-culture yogurt or kefir for a combination of prebiotics and probiotics.

According to recent reports, be sure to choose steel-cut whole oats instead of instant oats, which have less fiber and nutrients. Choose organic if possible. And, “bear in mind that a large proportion of the vitamins and trace elements are broken down during the cooking process,” notes Merkel, who adds that the healthiest way to eat oats is actually “uncooked.” If that sounds a little too rustic for you, he recommends the two alternatives below:.

To make the overnight oats, place oats in a small bowl and pour in a plant-based drink of your choice until the oats are completely covered. “Personally, I’m a big fan of unsweetened almond milk because it has the best nutritional value of all plant-based drinks and the taste also appeals to most people,” claims Merkel, who recommends enhancing the oats with nutritionally-rich spices such as cinnamon and turmeric. “Turmeric is rich in antioxidants and just a teaspoon is enough to make breakfast even healthier,” he says. Cover the oats and leave them to soak in the refrigerator for eight to twelve hours. “In the morning, you can add another superfood in the form of blueberries. Dark berries are also rich in antioxidants,” suggests Merkel. “If you prepare your oatmeal in this way, you have a super healthy breakfast that is rich in fiber and antioxidants and, unlike packaged muesli, only gently raises your insulin levels and keeps you full for a long time.”.

According to recent reports, merkel says oats can be easily added to your usual protein shake or smoothie for a boost of extra protein, nutrients, and fiber. “Add one to two tablespoons of uncooked rolled oats and some fresh fruit into the blender. The oats give the shake a pleasantly nutty taste and the vitamins are retained during the blending process,” he says.

It has been revealed that every Saturday from May to November, Great Barrington has a popular farmers’ market. Lines of local Berkshirites, visitors, little kids, and friendly dogs on leashes gather under packed canopies to buy a vibrant mix of fresh fruits, vegetables, flowers, and more. An older woman overheard me talking to my husband—in town for our end-of-summer vacation—about honeycrisps and insisted we go to the opposite end of the market to Maynard Farms’s booth. The family-owned orchard carries a diverse range of apples and “amazing stone fruits” she swore our excitable toddlers would love. She was right—the boys devoured nearly all of the produce before we left the market.

Last August, in the final warm days of summer, we drove winding highways through Hudson River mountains to the westernmost area of Massachusetts: a lush and culturally rich destination composed of 30 towns and two cities, collectively known as the Berkshires and located just two hours outside of Newly introduced York City.

In a recent development, lenox, the town we stayed in, is a quaint enclave that boasts multimillion-dollar Cape Cods, luxury day resorts, golfing, country clubs, and farm-to-table restaurants. It’s an ideal place for a weekend getaway with friends, a romantic escape, or a family trip with your littles to touch well-landscaped grass.

Sources indicate that we stayed in a newly built rental home, directly across the street from the Boston Symphony Orchestra at Tanglewood. In the evenings, if you’re within three miles of the parking lot, you can hear concerts from world-renowned artists. “Whether you're sitting in the front row enjoying James Taylor in the Koussevitzky Music Shed or sharing a candlelit picnic under the stars on the lawn, there is something magical about being here,” notes Amy Aldrich, senior director of patron experience at Tanglewood. “We take great pride in creating a welcoming atmosphere where world-class music and the beauty of nature come together to create something truly special.”.

Recent findings suggest that well-to-do families have long escaped the hustle of metropolitan Fresh England cities to decompress in the Berkshires because of its natural beauty. Author Edith Wharton, who chronicled the sordid lives of Gilded Age elites, built her 16,000-square-foot mansion and expansive garden estate in Lenox in 1902.

According to recent reports, back in the day, when affluent housewives needed a respite, they’d go to the “spa.” I never fully understood the older meaning of the term until I visited Miraval Berkshires, a 380-acre resort that boasts ancient Eastern treatments, healing equine therapy sessions, meditation classes, macronutrient dining, sound baths, astrological readings, and much more. It’s an adults-only, device-free space, so disconnecting from stress is mandatory.

Sources indicate that equestrian activities were a common theme for us during the trip. HomeFarm at Undermountain, run by executive director Lori Pestana, is a gem of a property. The animal sanctuary is dedicated to caring for and maintaining the health of horses—but also houses goats, sheep, and donkeys. “It’s a place where life slows down, where people reconnect with nature, with animals, and often with themselves,” Pestana says. “Whether visitors come to ride, explore, learn, or simply experience the peaceful rhythm of farm life, they leave with something they didn’t necessarily know they were looking for—a sense of belonging, joy, and connection.”.

Pestana’s small but dedicated staff offers riding lessons and a holistic view of what restoration can look like with a lot of care.

According to recent reports, for dining, expect most restaurants to serve farm-to-table dishes that are sourced from the seasonal produce and livestock being raised in the area. You couldn’t possibly get a closer farm-to-table experience than Highlawn Farms, which has delicious cheeses, ice cream, and milk made from the same cows grazing its property. It’s a general rule of thumb in my family that we never pass up the opportunity to have a wood-fired pizza—Pizzeria Boema has a chic Scandinavian interior and Fresh England quaint courtyard, serving the crispy, flavor-filled pies made with locally sourced mozzarella. And if you’re more interested in a fine-dining experience, Cello, run by couple Ryan and Kim Boya, takes a contemporary approach to comfort food. The 29-seat intimate restaurant has a thoughtfully curated menu of autochthonous plates like oyster mushroom pappardelle and a honey-nut squash served with goat cheese, pickled poblanos, granola, and a drizzle of hot honey.

Wildlife is ever-present in the Berkshires, from the calming transparently clear waters of Lenox Beach to the newly renovated aquarium wing of the Berkshire Museum in Pittsfield. Out the window of our car, driving from town to town, we saw peaceful creeks, grazing deer, and chirping birds. I soaked it all in, even stopping at the side of Glendale Road in Stockbridge to take in the beauty of the Housatonic River.

In recent years, because of the chaos of flying with toddlers, I’ve come to really appreciate the convenience of going to places just outside of New York City. I just want a soft life—or one as soft as humanly possible. With a good playlist on deck (we lean toward Afrojazz or Bad Bunny), we strap the kids into their car seats and roll. Open space and calm have to be on the itinerary.

There are many places we could go, but this experience in the Berkshires really stuck with me because it offered a quiet luxury that doesn’t position itself as high-maintenance or arrogant. There’s an ease and openness to this place, and if nothing else, an amazing peck of apples I’ll be looking forward to on my next visit.

It has been revealed that “It’s come to my attention that the hot girls are now eating peas,” Lainie Kates of Lainie Cooks indicates at the opening her video for the now-viral recipe for Tuscan Parmesan Peas. The beauty of green peas is that the legume is essentially as universal as cauliflower. A frozen bag from any supermarket (I have to say, the Trader Joe’s Petit Peas are my favorite, though perhaps it’s just a branding bias) can be whipped into a dip or added into almost any dish for a vegetarian source of both protein and fiber. It’s also a popular source for protein powder.

It seems that all of our childhood objections to the green vegetable were wrong—so this Thanksgiving, pass the peas, please.

Personally, I think we’ve been limiting Thanksgiving dinner to one holiday for far too long.

#146340. The Luxury Business of Las Vegas F1 Is Booming

The Luxury Business of Las Vegas F1 Is Booming

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1093 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If Formula 1 circuits were Mario Kart race tracks, the Las Vegas Grand Prix is as spiritually close to Rainbow Road as it gets.
  • This year, newly hybrid-engined F1 cars zoomed along an LED-lit Vegas Strip that had been closed off to civilian traffic each night of the event, much to the chagrin of every ride-share driver and/or tourist trying to cross Las Vegas Boulevard.
  • Max Verstappen, shortly after his win on Saturday night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If Formula 1 circuits were Mario Kart race tracks, the Las Vegas Grand Prix is as spiritually close to Rainbow Road as it gets.

This year, newly hybrid-engined F1 cars zoomed along an LED-lit Vegas Strip that had been closed off to civilian traffic each night of the event, much to the chagrin of every ride-share driver and/or tourist trying to cross Las Vegas Boulevard. They whipped past the Paris hotel casino’s glittering facsimile of the Eiffel Tower and the cartoonishly massive Sphere. They skirted under banners advertising Louis Vuitton and Qatar Airways. At the end, winner Max Verstappen was driven in a racing-striped stretch limousine, operated by a dashingly bedraggled Keanu Reeves, to the Fountains of Bellagio—inspired, like so many Vegas landmarks, by the architectural grandeur of Europe.

Max Verstappen, shortly after his win on Saturday night.

Motorsports enthusiast Keanu Reeves, center, drove the winners in a limo.

Since the Vegas GP was first revived in 2023, it has been a polarizing stop on the globe-trotting F1 calendar. (Back then, Verstappen called it “99 percent show and 1 percent sporting event.”) Even for a multibillion-dollar sport, was this too much glitz? Surrounded by sandy desert and snow-capped mountains, the gaudiest track in Formula 1 is nevertheless a sight to behold—and this year, it produced one of the most thrilling races in recent memory. Plus, as far as metropolises go, there are certainly more boring places to spend a few days than Sin City.

The winners’ podium: Red Bull’s Verstappen in first, followed by McLaren pair Lando Norris, left, and Oscar Piastri.

Well, unless you’re Kimi Antonelli, F1’s baby-faced world champ.

Recent findings suggest that “The thing I like the most here is the track, because I’m not allowed to do anything else other than drive around,” Antonelli told me, with a smirk, ahead of the race last week. “Because I’m not 21.”.

Sources indicate that (The Italian, who turned 20 in August, became Formula 1’s youngest-ever world champion at the Mexico Grand Prix earlier this month. In Vegas, he and his Mercedes teammate George Russell just missed the podium, finishing fourth and ninth respectively after more than a few late-race heartbreaks.).

Mercedes drivers Kimi Antonelli and George Russell.

In a recent development, but if you’re too old to wait in the line outside Marquee, there were plenty of other desirable libations afoot. Vegas has always been a place where fine cuisine (or at least, high-roller cuisine) means bumping up prices by dumping truffles and caviar on everything. The OG greats of modern dining—the Jean-Georges Vongerichtens and Wolfgang Pucks—have been here since the ’90s. But since COVID, a new generation of big-brass restaurateurs have set up shop on the Strip: Carbone Riviera and the Corner Store at the Bellagio’s properties; Sartiano’s and Delilah at the Wynn; Mother Wolf and Contramar at the Fontainebleau. (There are elite members’ clubs, too: Zero Bond opened at the Wynn in March.).

Brunch at Sadelle's, a popular Major Food Group spot, inside the Bellagio.

During Friday’s qualifying run, former F1 star Daniel Ricciardo stopped by the Corner Store at the Cosmopolitan, a wood-paneled outpost of the Latest York hotspot that opened a few weeks earlier. In the moody, multi-room space, the kitchen sends out platters of dry-aged wagyu and pepperoni pizza rolls while bartenders shake up sour-cream-and-onion martinis served with potato-chip sidecars. (The cocktail is purportedly Taylor Swift’s favorite, though executive chef Michael Vignola will neither confirm nor deny this: “I don’t know what you’re talking about,” stated Vignola, grinning. “You can also ask Travis.”).

Recent findings suggest that A day earlier, Ricciardo—who retired from F1 last year but came to town for a self-branded clothing pop-up and bar at the Bellagio—reflected on his own experience at the first-reprised Vegas GP in 2023. “It feels like a video game,” he said. “Whether the track is your favorite or not your favorite in terms of the actual layout, it’s still pretty surreal to be here and be the main event in a city that revolves around entertainment.”.

According to Vignola, Ricciardo is a substantial fan of the Corner Store’s steak program as well as the chicken paillard, “a sleeper on the menu and a great mid-course this year.” Manning the kitchen at the Corner Store in Vegas, which has 100 more seats than the original NYC location, the chef said they’re selling about as much caviar here as they do in Manhattan.

“Because of the volume here, we are slightly selling a little bit more caviar, slightly, you know, maybe 2 to 1,” Vignola said with a laugh. Lately, they’ve started R&D’ing some Norwegian king crab legs, including a prototype for a “crab appletini.” They’re leaning into menu items that the Fresh York-born chef described as “a little bit more Vegas, flashy kind of bespoke things. There are some high-roller dishes that pop off.”.

An Elvis impersonator at F1's Paddock Club.

The likes of Vignola and Mario Carbone, as well as the actual Wolfgang Puck and Jean-Georges, hosted caviar-filled pop-up stands at the Bellagio Fountain Club suites during the F1 festivities. The starriest celebrities, including Reeves and Kim Kardashian, who’s dating driver Lewis Hamilton, watched the significant race from the paddock, with a good view of the Elvis impersonator and humanoid robots who roamed the asphalt.

It has been revealed that over my few days in Vegas, multiple locals—including chefs, service and casino employees, and Uber and Lyft drivers—described how the city’s changed over the last 15 years. On the ride from the airport, my driver pointed to a new landmark on the horizon: a massive mirrored edifice shaped like the body of a guitar (the new Hard Rock Las Vegas hotel) that’s in the midst of being erected from the sand.

Recent findings suggest that “I think Vegas and Formula 1, they were meant for each other,” noted José Andrés, the Spanish-born chef who opened his first Las Vegas restaurants inside the then-freshly built Cosmopolitan in 2010. “I came here three weeks before the casino opened. And just to watch a casino open is the closest thing to watching a little egg hatch, or my daughter [being] born. For me to watch an entire casino from nothing to becoming a tower, it brings good memories.”.

One can only imagine how we’ll look back on the Las Vegas Grand Prix—only in its fourth year—a decade or two from now, when all the cars are self-driving and the Strip has been converted into an actual rainbow speedway floating in deep space. Will there still be Champagne?

According to recent reports, delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Whether it was roasting a chicken, pouring an outrageously large Cosmopolitan, or just organizing her pantry, I’d happily watch Ina Garten do just about anything on television. But there’s apparently one TV gig that even the Barefoot Contessa can't stomach, and I’m a little devastated we’ll never get to see it.

In a recent development, during the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, Garten got to talking with guest Rose Byrne about opportunities that felt too intimidating to pursue. Ina didn’t have to think very hard to come up with her own example.

“Somebody asked me to do Dancing with the Stars,” she revealed. “I thought, ‘Nobody needs to see that. That’s not happening.’”.

Recent findings suggest that with which I respectfully disagree. I think quite a few of us would happily clear our schedules to see Ina Garten attempt a salsa. Unfortunately, Garten wasn’t particularly eager to find out how she'd fare in the ballroom. “The closer I got to the day when I had to do it, the more I’d have nightmares,” she admitted.

Byrne was sympathetic, acknowledging that she’d be terrified of competing, too.

Industry observers note that still, this is a woman who’s made some pretty bold decisions throughout her career. Garten left her job working on nuclear energy policy in Washington, D.C., to buy a specialty food store in the Hamptons with virtually no experience running one. There were some early mishaps, including a batch of roast chickens nobody wanted until she changed how they were displayed, and those experiences eventually helped shape the approachable cooking philosophy behind her hugely successful cookbooks.

And Garten has certainly gotten comfortable sharing the spotlight over the years. In Delish’s recent interview with Garten and Jennifer Garner, the longtime friends traded stories about their kitchen adventures, favorite recipes, and even late-night In-N-Out Burger runs. Give Ina some good food and someone she loves spending time with, and she's in her element.

Personally, though, I can't stop imagining Jeffrey in the audience holding up a giant “10” sign in support of his wife. We really missed out on something special.

Tech Report: 9 Best Coffee Subscriptions, Reviewed & Reordered (2026)

⏱️ ~35 mins left to finish
